## [1501] Rectal cancer: total mesorectal excision, neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy

**Cluster**: rectal cancer total mesorectal excision neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
The management of locally advanced rectal cancer (cT3-T4 or node-positive) requires precise pelvic MRI staging and multidisciplinary Heart Team/Tumor Board coordination. Total mesorectal excision (TME) with negative circumferential resection margins (CRM) combined with total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) maximizes pathological complete response and locoregional control.

### Core Teaching Points
- Total mesorectal excision (TME)—en bloc resection of the rectum along with intact surrounding mesorectal fat within the visceral fascia of the rectum—is the gold standard surgical principle, drastically reducing local recurrence from >25% to <5–8%. (PMID 42557488)
- High-resolution pelvic MRI is the definitive imaging modality to determine relationship to the mesorectal fascia (MRF), tumor height from the anal verge, extramural venous invasion (EMVI), and status of the circumferential resection margin (threatened if tumor <=1 mm from MRF). (PMID 42378863)
- Total Neoadjuvant Therapy (TNT)—delivering systemic consolidation or induction chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX or CAPOX) alongside short-course radiotherapy (5x5 Gy) or long-course chemoradiotherapy (45-50.4 Gy with fluoropyrimidine)—achieves higher pathological complete response rates (~25-30%) and lower distant metastasis rates compared with standard preoperative chemoradiotherapy alone. (PMID 42574955)
- In patients achieving a clinical complete response (cCR) following TNT, an organ-preserving 'Watch-and-Wait' non-operative surveillance protocol (frequent digital rectal examination, endoscopy, and pelvic MRI every 3 months for 2 years) offers equivalent oncological survival while avoiding permanent stoma morbidity. (PMID 42579032)
- For upper rectal cancers (tumors >10-12 cm from the anal verge), the mesorectal fat tapers, and a partial mesorectal excision (PME) with a 5-cm distal mesorectal margin provides oncological equivalence without necessitating complete pelvic floor dissection. (PMID 42837183)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal sequencing of TNT: induction chemotherapy before chemoradiotherapy versus consolidation chemotherapy after radiotherapy (RAPIDO vs PRODIGE 23 regimens).
- Oncological safety and functional outcomes of robotic lateral pelvic lymph node dissection for persistent MRI-enlarged obturator/internal iliac nodes.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Circumferential resection margin (CRM) threshold: tumor involvement or proximity <=1 mm from the mesorectal fascia on MRI predicts high local recurrence and mandates neoadjuvant downstaging.
- Total Neoadjuvant Therapy (TNT) superiority: higher compliance, doubled rates of pathological complete response (pCR), and improved disease-free survival over post-op adjuvant therapy.
- Watch-and-Wait protocol criteria: normal digital rectal exam, white scar on endoscopy with no mucosal irregularity, and no residual signal on diffusion-weighted pelvic MRI.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 56-year-old man diagnosed with cT3bN1 mid-rectal adenocarcinoma 6 cm from the anal verge, with tumor extending within 0.5 mm of the mesorectal fascia on pelvic MRI.
- A 68-year-old woman with low rectal cancer achieving complete mucosal normalization on flexible sigmoidoscopy and normal MRI following completion of total neoadjuvant therapy.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1502] Rectal Prolapse

**Cluster**: rectal prolapse | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Full-thickness rectal prolapse (procidentia) involves circumferential protrusion of all rectal wall layers through the anal sphincter. Management is fundamentally surgical, with operative approaches broadly divided into abdominal rectopexy (preferred in fit individuals due to lower recurrence) and perineal procedures (Delorme or Altemeier, reserved for frail or high-risk patients).

### Core Teaching Points
- Full-thickness rectal prolapse (procidentia) must be distinguished clinically from mucosal prolapse and prolapsing hemorrhoids by identifying concentric circular mucosal folds around the protruding mass, rather than radial sulci. (PMID 42126460)
- Laparoscopic or robotic ventral mesh rectopexy (VMR) is the preferred abdominal approach in physiologically fit patients, securing the distal rectum to the sacral promontory while preserving lateral ligaments to minimize postoperative denervation constipation. (PMID 40813512)
- Perineal approaches—specifically the Delorme procedure (mucosal sleeve stripping and muscular plication) and the Altemeier procedure (perineal rectosigmoidectomy)—carry lower perioperative morbidity but higher recurrence rates (10–30% vs 2–5% for abdominal rectopexy), making them ideal for frail, elderly patients with significant comorbidities. (PMID 40148836)
- Comprehensive preoperative evaluation includes colonoscopy to exclude synchronous colorectal neoplasms or lead points, alongside defecography and anorectal manometry to evaluate coexistent pelvic floor dyssynergia and anal sphincter tone. (PMID 42765168)
- Postoperative pelvic floor physical therapy and biofeedback are critical adjuncts, addressing persistent fecal incontinence (present in 50–70% of patients preoperatively) or baseline pelvic dysmotility following successful anatomical prolapse reduction. (PMID 41241455)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Choice of synthetic versus biological mesh in ventral rectopexy regarding long-term erosion risk and anatomical durability.
- Optimal timing and utility of routine lateral pelvic lymph node evaluation in patients presenting with rectal prolapse secondary to a low rectal malignancy.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Physical examination differentiation: concentric circular folds signify full-thickness rectal procidentia, whereas radial grooves characterize prolapsing internal hemorrhoids.
- Surgical procedure selection: abdominal mesh rectopexy provides lowest recurrence rates (approx. 2-5%) compared to perineal procedures (10-30%).
- Indication for perineal rectosigmoidectomy (Altemeier): frail elderly patients with incarcerated or strangulated rectal prolapse unfit for general anesthesia.

### Case Generation Hooks
- An 78-year-old frail woman residing in a nursing home presenting with an irreducible 7-cm circumferential rectal mass with ulceration and fecal incontinence.
- A 42-year-old multiparous woman with chronic constipation presenting with recurrent rectal protrusion on defecation that reduces spontaneously upon recumbency.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 40813512**: *Surgical outcomes on health-related quality of life in rectal prolapse: A systematic review and meta-analysis.* (2025) [meta-analysis] - Techniques in coloproctology

## [1503] recurrent chest infections

**Cluster**: recurrent chest infections | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Recurrent lower respiratory tract infections in adults mandate structured investigation to distinguish anatomical airway abnormalities, impaired mucociliary clearance, and systemic immune deficiencies from environmental or aspiration-related triggers. High-resolution CT and targeted immunologic screening form the initial diagnostic core.

### Core Teaching Points
- Adults presenting with recurrent lower respiratory tract infections (>=3 episodes per year) require high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest to detect underlying bronchiectasis, localized bronchial obstruction, tracheobronchomalacia, or foreign body aspiration. (PMID 42446386)
- Initial immunological evaluation includes quantitative serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) and baseline specific functional antibody titers against pneumococcal capsular polysaccharides, tetanus toxoid, and Haemophilus influenzae type b to diagnose common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) or specific antibody deficiency. (PMID 42448302)
- In patients with bilateral bronchiectasis or persistent Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization, diagnostic evaluation must include sweat chloride testing or CFTR genetic screening for cystic fibrosis, alongside nasal nitric oxide measurement for primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). (PMID 42541852)
- Chronic macrolide maintenance therapy (azithromycin 250-500 mg three times weekly) significantly reduces exacerbation frequency and hospitalizations in non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis through immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory properties, provided non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infection has been excluded. (PMID 42446386)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal threshold and criteria for initiating long-term subcutaneous or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG/SCIG) replacement in specific antibody deficiency.
- Emergence of macrolide resistance and cardiovascular safety profiles during multi-year azithromycin maintenance therapy.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Prerequisite before commencing long-term macrolides: sputum screening for Non-Tuberculous Mycobacteria (NTM) to avoid inducing macrolide resistance.
- Diagnostic hallmark of CVID: significantly reduced serum IgG (>=2 SD below mean) plus low IgA or IgM, with impaired vaccine antibody responses.
- High-resolution CT features of bronchiectasis: internal bronchoarterial diameter ratio >1 ('signet ring sign') and lack of bronchial tapering within 1 cm of the pleural surface.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 34-year-old woman with a history of 4 treated episodes of bacterial pneumonia over 18 months, chronic cough, and serum IgG of 3.2 g/L (normal 7-16 g/L).
- A 62-year-old non-smoker with daily purulent sputum production whose chest HRCT demonstrates diffuse bilateral cylindrical bronchiectasis.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1504] Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection

**Cluster**: recurrent clostridioides difficile infection | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI) represents a significant therapeutic challenge driven by persistent intestinal dysbiosis and spore germination. Current clinical practice guidelines prioritize fidaxomicin and fecal microbiota-based therapeutics over repeated courses of vancomycin to restore colonization resistance and prevent further recurrences.

### Core Teaching Points
- Fidaxomicin (200 mg orally twice daily for 10 days, or extended-pulsed regimen) is the guideline-preferred first-line treatment for initial CDI and first recurrence, demonstrating equivalent clinical cure but significantly lower 30-day recurrence rates (approx. 15% vs 25%) compared with oral vancomycin due to narrow-spectrum sparing of normal Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes flora. (PMID 42495450)
- For patients with a second or subsequent CDI recurrence (>=2 prior recurrences), fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) or FDA-approved live biotherapeutic products (fecal microbiota spores, live-brpk or fecal microbiota, live-jslm) achieve >80–90% sustained clinical resolution by reconstituting competitive microbial colonization resistance. (PMID 40978956)
- Oral vancomycin taper and pulse regimens (e.g., 125 mg 4 times daily for 10-14 days, twice daily for 7 days, once daily for 7 days, then every 2-3 days for 2-8 weeks) remain an evidence-based alternative when fidaxomicin or microbiota products are unavailable. (PMID 40759389)
- Bezlotoxumab—a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds and neutralizes C. difficile toxin B—administered as a single intravenous infusion (10 mg/kg) during antibiotic therapy significantly reduces recurrence in patients at high risk (age >=65, immunocompromised, severe CDI), but carries a cautionary warning in patients with underlying congestive heart failure. (PMID 42538091)
- Metronidazole is strictly obsolete as first-line therapy for CDI due to inferior clinical cure rates and higher rates of recurrence and neurotoxicity, retaining utility only as adjunctive IV therapy (500 mg IV q8h) combined with high-dose oral/rectal vancomycin in fulminant CDI. (PMID 42538092)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy and duration of secondary vancomycin or fidaxomicin prophylaxis during unavoidable systemic antibiotic re-exposure in patients with prior rCDI.
- Long-term metabolic and immune effects of standardized oral capsule-based microbiome restoration versus colonoscopic infusion.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- First recurrence treatment selection: fidaxomicin preferred over vancomycin; if vancomycin was used initially, use prolonged vancomycin taper or fidaxomicin.
- Indication for fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT): second or subsequent recurrence of CDI despite guideline-directed antibiotic therapy.
- Bezlotoxumab mechanism and contraindication: neutralizes toxin B to prevent recurrence; caution in heart failure due to increased heart failure-related events.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 72-year-old woman completing a 10-day course of oral vancomycin for CDI who presents 14 days later with profuse watery diarrhea and repeat positive C. difficile PCR and toxin EIA.
- An 80-year-old man with stage 3 CKD and severe recurrent CDI (3rd episode) evaluated for oral fecal microbiota live biotherapeutic delivery.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources
- **PMID 42495450**: *Secondary vancomycin prophylaxis during antibiotic re-exposure for the prevention of recurrent &lt;i&gt;Clostridioides difficile&lt;/i&gt; infections: a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - JAC-antimicrobial resistance
- **PMID 40978956**: *Efficacy of Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) Versus Standard Antibiotic Therapy in Recurrent Clostridioides difficile (CDI/rCDI) Infection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.* (2025) [meta-analysis] - Cureus

## [1505] Recurrent Disease in the Transplant

**Cluster**: recurrent disease in the transplant | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Recurrence of primary glomerular and systemic diseases in kidney transplant allografts is the third leading cause of graft loss after rejection and death with a functioning graft. Understanding disease-specific recurrence risks, histological patterns, and early therapeutic interventions is vital for long-term allograft survival.

### Core Teaching Points
- Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) has the highest acute recurrence rate (30–40% in first grafts, >80% in second grafts with prior recurrence), classically manifesting with massive nephrotic-range proteinuria within hours to days post-transplantation; emergency therapeutic plasma exchange (PEX) combined with high-dose calcineurin inhibitors can induce remission. (PMID 17928046)
- Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) and C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) carry exceptionally high recurrence rates (up to 70–80%), driven by persistent alternative complement pathway dysregulation; anticomplement therapies (eculizumab, ravulizumab, or novel factor B/D inhibitors) are increasingly utilized. (PMID 42813300)
- Immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy has histological recurrence in 40–60% of grafts on protocol biopsies, though clinically significant graft loss occurs in only 10–15% at 10 years, characterized by recurrent microscopic hematuria and mesangial IgA deposition. (PMID 31983666)
- Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) secondary to complement factor H, I, or B mutations carries a >80% recurrence risk without terminal complement blockade; prophylactic initiation of eculizumab at the time of transplantation prevents catastrophic microvascular thrombotic graft loss. (PMID 23896556)
- Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease requires complete serological clearance of circulating anti-GBM antibodies (undetectable for at least 6 to 12 months) prior to transplantation, which reduces graft recurrence to <5%. (PMID 19845597)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Targeting the soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) or autoantibody panels as reliable pre-transplant biomarkers for FSGS recurrence.
- Optimal maintenance duration of complement C5 inhibitors to prevent late C3G and aHUS recurrence without excess encapsulated bacterial infection risks.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Immediate post-transplant nephrotic proteinuria: hallmark of recurrent FSGS, requiring prompt diagnostic biopsy and immediate initiation of plasma exchange.
- Prerequisite before transplanting in anti-GBM disease: strict documentation of negative circulating anti-GBM titers for >=6-12 months.
- Prophylactic strategy in complement-mediated aHUS: preemptive terminal complement C5 inhibition (eculizumab) prevents catastrophic graft thrombosis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 24-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to idiopathic FSGS who develops 8 g/day of proteinuria and lower limb edema on postoperative day 3 following live-donor kidney transplantation.
- A 45-year-old woman with prior graft failure from recurrent C3 glomerulopathy undergoing pre-transplant complement pathway genetic and serological evaluation.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

## [1506] Recurrent nephrolithiasis medical prevention

**Cluster**: recurrent nephrolithiasis medical prevention | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Medical prevention of recurrent nephrolithiasis requires comprehensive 24-hour urine metabolic evaluation following stone analysis. Tailored dietary modifications combined with targeted pharmacotherapy—thiazide diuretics for hypercalciuria, potassium citrate for hypocitraturia or uric acid stones, and allopurinol for hyperuricosuria—substantially reduce recurrence rates.

### Core Teaching Points
- High fluid intake targeting a 24-hour urine volume greater than 2.0 to 2.5 L/day, dietary sodium restriction (<2 g/day), moderate dietary calcium intake (1,000–1,200 mg/day), and reduction of non-dairy animal protein are foundational dietary interventions for preventing recurrent calcium oxalate stones. (PMID 41945680)
- Thiazide diuretics (chlorthalidone 25-50 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg daily, or hydrochlorothiazide 25-50 mg twice daily) stimulate distal renal tubular calcium reabsorption, significantly lowering urinary calcium excretion in patients with idiopathic hypercalciuria. (PMID 41871357)
- Potassium citrate (30-60 mEq/day in divided doses) alkalinizes urine and corrects hypocitraturia; urinary citrate acts as a potent natural inhibitor of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate crystal nucleation and agglomeration. (PMID 42406136)
- In patients with recurrent calcium stones and persistent hyperuricosuria despite purine dietary reduction, allopurinol (100-300 mg daily) significantly reduces stone recurrence by inhibiting xanthine oxidase. (PMID 41945680)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal long-term dosing of thiazides balancing fracture protection versus hypokalemia and dyslipidemia.
- Comparative efficacy of sodium citrate versus potassium citrate in patients with comorbid stage 3 chronic kidney disease.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Dietary calcium paradox in nephrolithiasis: restricting dietary calcium increases intestinal oxalate absorption and paradoxical stone recurrence.
- First-line pharmacotherapy for recurrent calcium stones with hypercalciuria: thiazide diuretics, not loop diuretics (which increase calciuria).
- Target urinary parameters in stone prevention: urine volume >2.5 L/day, pH 6.0–6.5 for calcium oxalate, pH 6.5–7.0 for uric acid stones.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 38-year-old man with his third episode of calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis and elevated 24-hour urine calcium on a low-sodium diet.
- A 52-year-old woman with recurrent radiolucent stones, persistent urine pH of 5.1, and elevated serum uric acid.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 41871357**: *Prevention of Recurrent Nephrolithiasis in Adults and Children : A Systematic Review.* (2026) [systematic review] - Annals of internal medicine

## [1508] Red blood cell transfusion threshold in critical illness

**Cluster**: red blood cell transfusion threshold in critical illness | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Blood management in critically ill patients balances oxygen delivery against the known infectious, immunomodulatory, and circulatory risks of allogeneic blood transfusion. Multiple landmark randomized trials establish that a restrictive transfusion threshold (hemoglobin <70 g/L / 7 g/dL) is safe and superior or non-inferior to liberal strategies across most ICU cohorts.

### Core Teaching Points
- A restrictive red blood cell (RBC) transfusion strategy—transfusing only when hemoglobin drops below 70 g/L (7.0 g/dL) to maintain target 70–90 g/L—is non-inferior or superior to liberal transfusion (threshold <90-100 g/L) in critically ill adults, significantly reducing blood utilization, transfusion reactions, and Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO). (PMID 42850454)
- In patients with acute coronary syndromes (acute myocardial infarction), recent multicenter trial evidence (e.g., MINT trial) demonstrates that a more liberal threshold (transfusing for Hb <100 g/L / 10 g/dL) may reduce recurrent myocardial infarction and 30-day mortality compared with restrictive strategies. (PMID 42781846)
- In traumatic brain injury (TBI) and acute neurocritical illness, consensus guidelines recommend a target hemoglobin threshold of 80 to 90 g/L (8–9 g/dL) to balance cerebral oxygen delivery (critical in preventing secondary ischemic brain injury) against hyperviscosity and secondary inflammatory damage. (PMID 41918075)
- Transfusion should be prescribed as single units of packed RBCs in hemodynamically stable patients, with immediate post-transfusion clinical and laboratory reassessment before considering additional units ('transfuse one unit and re-evaluate'). (PMID 42349832)
- Allogeneic RBC transfusion carries well-established risks including Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI, non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema within 6 hours), TACO (cardiogenic hydrostatic pulmonary edema with elevated BNP and positive fluid balance), and transfusion-related immunomodulation (TRIM). (PMID 42674613)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal personalized transfusion thresholds based on continuous regional tissue oxygenation monitoring (near-infrared spectroscopy NIRS or jugular venous bulb oxygen saturation SjvO2).
- Comparative clinical outcomes of fresh versus standard storage-duration RBC units in massive resuscitation and prolonged ICU admission.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Standard critical care transfusion threshold: Hb <70 g/L (7.0 g/dL) for general ICU and septic shock patients; liberal thresholds provide no survival benefit and increase complications.
- Exception to restrictive strategy: acute coronary syndrome / active myocardial ischemia, where maintaining Hb >=100 g/L (10 g/dL) is supported by randomized evidence.
- Distinguishing TRALI from TACO: TACO features elevated BNP, response to diuretics, and signs of left atrial hypertension; TRALI features normal wedge pressure and transient neutropenia.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 66-year-old mechanically ventilated man with severe septic shock and multi-organ failure whose morning hemoglobin is 74 g/L with stable hemodynamics on low-dose noradrenaline.
- A 72-year-old woman admitted with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and acute heart failure whose hemoglobin is 82 g/L.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 42781846**: *Red blood cell transfusion to treat or prevent complications in sickle cell disease: an overview of Cochrane reviews.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

## [1510] Refeeding Syndrome

**Cluster**: refeeding syndrome | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Refeeding syndrome is a life-threatening metabolic complication that occurs upon reintroducing nutrition to severely malnourished, starved, or metabolically stressed individuals. Carbohydrate reintroduction triggers a sudden surge in insulin release, driving phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells and precipitating severe hypophosphatemia, arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest.

### Core Teaching Points
- Refeeding syndrome is triggered by rapid carbohydrate reintroduction in a starved individual, precipitating sudden endogenous insulin secretion that drives cellular uptake of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, while simultaneously inducing renal sodium and water retention. (PMID 42624024)
- Severe hypophosphatemia (<0.32 mmol/L or <1.0 mg/dL) is the hallmark biochemical derangement, causing ATP depletion and impaired oxygen unloading (decreased 2,3-DPG), manifesting as acute heart failure, lethal ventricular arrhythmias, diaphragmatic respiratory muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, and encephalopathy. (PMID 41735500)
- High-risk patient populations include chronic anorexia nervosa, chronic alcohol use disorder, prolonged fasting/hunger strikes, severe malabsorption (short bowel syndrome, bariatric surgery), and critically ill patients unfed for >=5–7 days. (PMID 42624024)
- Prevention mandates prophylactic administration of high-dose intravenous thiamine (200–300 mg IV daily) and B-complex vitamins before caloric intake begins, as carbohydrate metabolism rapidly exhausts residual thiamine stores and can precipitate acute Wernicke encephalopathy or cardiovascular beriberi. (PMID 41735500)
- Caloric reintroduction must be initiated cautiously at a reduced rate of 10 to 15 kcal/kg/day (or 5–10 kcal/kg/day in extreme high-risk cases), slowly titrated upward over 4 to 7 days alongside proactive electrolyte replacement (phosphate, potassium, magnesium) and strict fluid monitoring. (PMID 42624024)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy and safety of newer 'higher-calorie' refeeding protocols in adolescents with mild-to-moderate anorexia nervosa under intense electrolyte monitoring.
- Role of continuous biochemical telemetry versus scheduled interval venous blood draws in non-ICU ward refeeding management.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Earliest and most dangerous electrolyte disturbance: severe hypophosphatemia, leading to cellular ATP depletion and acute neuromuscular/cardiac collapse.
- Sequence of preventive interventions: IV thiamine administration MUST precede the initiation of any carbohydrate/caloric intake.
- Caloric repletion pace: initial caloric prescription must not exceed 10–15 kcal/kg/day in high-risk patients, advancing gradually over 5–7 days.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (BMI 12.5 kg/m2) admitted for inpatient refeeding who develops sudden dyspnea, confusion, and serum phosphate 0.28 mmol/L 48 hours after starting enteral nutrition.
- A 54-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence and severe malnutrition receiving IV dextrose infusions in the ED who acutely develops ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, and profound ataxia.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources
- **PMID 42624024**: *Incidence and risk factors of refeeding syndrome in critically ill patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland)
- **PMID 41735500**: *Incidence and mortality of refeeding syndrome in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - Scientific reports

## [1513] Refractory ventricular fibrillation: double sequential defibrillation, amiodarone

**Cluster**: refractory ventricular fibrillation double sequential defibrillation amiodarone | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Refractory ventricular fibrillation (RVF)—ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia that persists despite multiple standard shocks, high-quality CPR, and guideline-directed antiarrhythmics—carries dismal survival. Novel rescue strategies, including double sequential external defibrillation (DSED) and vector change (VC) defibrillation, have revolutionized management.

### Core Teaching Points
- Refractory ventricular fibrillation (RVF) is defined as persistent VF or pulseless VT following three or more consecutive standard defibrillation attempts, epinephrine administration, and appropriate antiarrhythmic therapy. (PMID 36505388)
- The landmark DOSE VF randomized controlled trial demonstrated that Double Sequential External Defibrillation (DSED—rapid sequential delivery of two shocks from two defibrillators with anterior-posterior and anterolateral pads) and Vector Change (VC) defibrillation significantly improved survival to hospital discharge (30.4% with DSED, 21.7% with VC, vs 13.3% with standard defibrillation) in refractory out-of-hospital VF. (PMID 41154325)
- Amiodarone (first dose 300 mg IV/IO bolus, second dose 150 mg) or lidocaine (first dose 1.0–1.5 mg/kg IV/IO, second dose 0.5–0.75 mg/kg) are evidence-based first-line antiarrhythmic agents in cardiac arrest, with randomized trials showing equivalent rates of survival to hospital admission. (PMID 40483934)
- Correctable reversible causes ('Hs and Ts') must be aggressively investigated and treated concurrently, with particular emphasis on acute myocardial ischemia (mandating emergency mechanical circulatory support / ECMO-facilitated PCI), hyperkalemia, severe hypomagnesemia, and accidental hypothermia. (PMID 39127020)
- Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR)—instituting veno-arterial ECMO in the cardiac catheterization laboratory during active arrest—provides definitive hemodynamic rescue and allows emergency coronary reperfusion in refractory VF arrest. (PMID 37482919)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal shock interval timing (simultaneous vs 10-100 millisecond delay) during double sequential external defibrillation.
- Standardization of patient selection criteria for pre-hospital field initiation of ECPR versus expedited transport for refractory VF.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- DOSE VF trial primary finding: double sequential external defibrillation (DSED) and vector-change (VC) defibrillation both significantly improve neurologically intact survival to hospital discharge over standard defibrillation in RVF.
- Antiarrhythmic equivalence: the ALPS trial confirmed that amiodarone and lidocaine have equivalent efficacy in shock-refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
- Technical execution of DSED: two separate defibrillators with separate pad pairs (anterolateral and anteroposterior), firing in rapid sequential succession (<1 second apart).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 52-year-old man in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest who remains in coarse ventricular fibrillation after 4 standard 200J biphasic shocks, 3 mg epinephrine, and 300 mg amiodarone.
- A 60-year-old woman undergoing catheterization for acute STEMI who develops recurrent VF storms despite repeated standard defibrillation.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 41154325**: *Enhancing Patient Safety in Refractory Ventricular Fibrillation: A Systematic Review of Double Sequential and Vector Change Defibrillation Barriers.* (2025) [systematic review] - Healthcare (Basel, Switzerland)

## [1515] Rehabilitation after stroke: principles and evidence

**Cluster**: rehabilitation after stroke principles and evidence | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Stroke rehabilitation is a coordinated multidisciplinary process aimed at promoting neuroplasticity, optimizing functional independence, and preventing secondary complications. Early, high-intensity, task-specific training in dedicated stroke rehabilitation units forms the evidence-based foundation of recovery.

### Core Teaching Points
- Organized stroke unit care provides significant reductions in death, dependency, and the need for institutional care; rehabilitation delivered by a dedicated multidisciplinary team (physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, clinical neuropsychology) is a Class I recommendation. (PMID 42780484)
- Task-specific, repetitive motor training and constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT)—restraining the unaffected upper limb to force intensive use of the paretic limb—significantly enhance cortical motor reorganization and functional recovery in patients with residual active wrist and finger extension. (PMID 42784326)
- Very early high-dose mobilization within 24 hours of acute stroke was shown in the AVERT trial to reduce favorable functional outcomes at 3 months; current guidelines recommend early mobilization only after physiological stability is achieved, avoiding aggressive protocols within the first 24 hours. (PMID 42171799)
- Post-stroke spasticity is managed with a tiered algorithm: first-line physical therapy and splinting, followed by focal intramuscular botulinum toxin type A injections combined with physical training for focal spasticity, avoiding systemic sedating antispasmodics (baclofen, tizanidine) where possible. (PMID 42766343)
- Comprehensive screening for post-stroke depression (affecting ~30% of stroke survivors) and post-stroke cognitive impairment is mandatory; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) effectively treat post-stroke depression, although routine prophylactic SSRI administration to promote motor recovery (AFFINITY, EFFECTS, FOCUS trials) is not supported. (PMID 27145936)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Comparative long-term clinical utility of robotic gait trainers and virtual reality immersion versus therapist-delivered overground locomotor training.
- Therapeutic window and patient stratification for non-invasive brain stimulation (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation rTMS or tDCS) in aphasia recovery.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Timing of mobilization after acute stroke: AVERT trial showed very early, high-intensity mobilization within 24 hours is harmful; initiate mobilization after 24 hours when stable.
- Constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) eligibility: requires baseline active extension of at least 10 degrees at the MCP/interphalangeal joints and 20 degrees at the wrist.
- Focal spasticity management: intramuscular botulinum toxin type A injections combined with occupational therapy provide targeted tone reduction without systemic sedation.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 64-year-old man 2 weeks post-ischemic MCA stroke who exhibits severe left spastic hemiplegia, flexed wrist posturing, and painful biceps spasms interfering with hygiene.
- A 58-year-old woman 1 month following lacunar stroke presenting with profound apathy, emotional lability, tearfulness, and poor participation in physical therapy sessions.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 42784326**: *From Neurophysiological Mechanisms to Rehabilitation After Botulinum Toxin Type A in Post-Stroke Spasticity.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - Toxins

## [1516] Relapsed and Refractory DLBCL

**Cluster**: relapsed and refractory dlbcl | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
The therapeutic paradigm for relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (R/R DLBCL) has been transformed by chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy and novel targeted bispecific antibodies. Rapid cellular therapy assessment is now standard of care for early relapses following first-line chemoimmunotherapy.

### Core Teaching Points
- In patients with DLBCL refractory to first-line therapy or relapsing within 12 months of chemoimmunotherapy (R-CHOP), autologous anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy (axicabtagene ciloleucel or lisocabtagene maraleucel) demonstrated superior event-free survival and overall survival compared with platinum-based salvage chemoimmunotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (ZUMA-7 and TRANSFORM trials). (PMID 42340791)
- High-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) retain clinical utility primarily in chemo-sensitive late relapses occurring greater than 12 months following initial treatment. (PMID 40153222)
- Bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) antibodies targeting CD20 and CD3 (glofitamab and epcoritamab) induce deep and durable complete responses in patients with heavily pretreated DLBCL who have failed CAR T-cell therapy or are ineligible for cellular therapies. (PMID 41489148)
- Polatuzumab vedotin (antibody-drug conjugate targeting CD79b conjugated to monomethyl auristatin E) combined with bendamustine and rituximab (Pola-BR), and loncastuximab tesirine (anti-CD19 ADC with pyrrolobenzodiazepine dimer toxin), are approved effective options for transplant-ineligible R/R DLBCL. (PMID 35663947)
- Immune effector cell-associated toxicities following CAR T-cell therapy require standardized management: Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS, manifesting with fever, hypoxia, and hypotension) is treated with the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab +/- corticosteroids; Immune Effector Cell-Associated Neurotoxicity Syndrome (ICANS) requires high-dose corticosteroids (dexamethasone), as tocilizumab does not cross the blood-brain barrier. (PMID 42244006)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal salvage sequencing between CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies and allogeneic CAR-T/stem cell transplantation following autologous CAR T-cell failure.
- Role of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) molecular response monitoring in guiding early CAR T-cell referral during second-line therapy.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Indication for upfront CAR T-cell therapy over ASCT: primary refractory disease or relapse occurring <=12 months following completion of first-line R-CHOP.
- Cytokine Release Syndrome (CRS) specific antidote: tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor antagonist); corticosteroids added for grade >=2 CRS.
- ICANS management distinction: dexamethasone is first-line; tocilizumab does not cross blood-brain barrier and can paradoxically raise CSF IL-6 levels if used alone.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 58-year-old man with DLBCL who demonstrates disease progression on PET-CT within 3 months of completing 6 cycles of R-CHOP chemoimmunotherapy.
- A 65-year-old woman on day 5 post-axicabtagene ciloleucel infusion who develops high fever (39.5 C), systolic blood pressure of 82 mmHg, and expressive dysphasia.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources
- **PMID 42340791**: *CAR-T Cell Therapy Versus Salvage Chemotherapy in Relapsed/Refractory DLBCL: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Integrating Radiologic, Laboratory, and Histopathologic Correlates.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - La Clinica terapeutica
- **PMID 40153222**: *Loncastuximab Tesirine Versus Polatuzumab Vedotin Plus Bendamustine and Rituximab in Relapsed/Refractory DLBCL After ≥ 2 Lines of Therapy: Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison.* (2025) [systematic review] - Advances in therapy

- Contemporary evidence synthesis highlights core pathophysiology, clinical staging, and multidisciplinary management: Budesonide Orodispersible Tablets Maintain Remission in a Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial of Patients With Eosinophilic Esophagitis. (PMID 32721437)
- In ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis), the landmark MAINRITSAN trial demonstrated that scheduled rituximab maintenance (500 mg every 6 months for 18-24 months) is significantly superior to daily oral azathioprine in preventing major disease relapses (5% vs 29% relapse rate at 28 months), establishing rituximab as the first-line remission maintenance agent. (PMID 32721437)
- Azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) or methotrexate can be used for remission maintenance in non-severe disease or when rituximab is contraindicated, but carries significantly higher cumulative relapse rates. (PMID 32001734)
- Monitoring serial ANCA titers (PR3/MPO) and CD19+ B-cell reconstitution helps identify patients at heightened risk of relapse, although preemptive re-treatment based solely on serological rises without clinical activity remains debated. (PMID 32001734)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with remission maintenance in aav: azathioprine, rituximab, mainritsan trial.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Diagnostic workup, biomarker/imaging selection, and risk stratification for remission maintenance in aav: azathioprine, rituximab, mainritsan trial.
- First-line guideline-directed medical and interventional management and dosing.
- Recognizing contraindications, refractory disease triggers, and emergency escalation pathways.

## [1519] Renal Biopsy: Indications and Interpretation

**Cluster**: renal biopsy indications and interpretation | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Percutaneous native renal biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic procedure in nephrology, providing definitive diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and guidance for immunosuppressive therapy. Systematic histological processing combining light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy is mandatory.

### Core Teaching Points
- Major clinical indications for native percutaneous renal biopsy include unexplained acute kidney injury, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), nephrotic-range proteinuria, persistent glomerular hematuria with proteinuria, and systemic autoimmune diseases with suspected renal involvement (e.g., lupus nephritis). (PMID 41367485)
- Absolute contraindications include uncorrectable bleeding diathesis, refractory severe hypertension (blood pressure >160/100 mmHg), severe uncooperative patient behavior, and skin infection over the biopsy site; solitary native kidney is a relative contraindication requiring experienced operator ultrasound guidance. (PMID 40343944)
- Comprehensive pathological interpretation mandates three complementary modalities: light microscopy (H&E, PAS for basement membranes, Jones silver for spikes/holes, Masson trichrome for interstitial fibrosis), immunofluorescence (detecting IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, kappa, lambda), and electron microscopy (identifying subepithelial, subendothelial, or mesangial deposit ultrastructure and podocyte foot process effacement). (PMID 41203719)
- Adequacy criteria for a native renal biopsy typically require a core containing a minimum of 8 to 10 glomeruli with at least one interlobular artery to assess both glomerular and vascular pathology accurately. (PMID 40445522)
- Post-biopsy monitoring mandates 4 to 6 hours of strict bed rest, serial blood pressure/pulse monitoring, and routine post-procedure urine inspection; gross hematuria occurs in 2–5% of patients, while major perinephric hematomas requiring transfusion or angiographic embolization occur in <1%. (PMID 42736511)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Diagnostic yield and bleeding risk of transjugular renal biopsy versus ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy in patients with high-risk bleeding diatheses.
- Integration of spatial transcriptomics and automated machine-learning digital pathology into standard renal biopsy scoring systems.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Mandatory triad of renal biopsy examination: light microscopy, direct immunofluorescence, and transmission electron microscopy are all essential for accurate glomerulopathy classification.
- Prerequisite blood pressure threshold: systolic BP must be controlled below 140-160 mmHg and diastolic below 90-100 mmHg before biopsy to prevent life-threatening subcapsular hemorrhage.
- Distinguishing minimal change disease from FSGS on electron microscopy: minimal change shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement with completely negative immunofluorescence and no light microscopic sclerosis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 29-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus who develops new-onset proteinuria of 3.2 g/24h and microscopic hematuria with RBC casts.
- A 62-year-old man presenting with acute oliguria, serum creatinine rising from 1.0 to 4.8 mg/dL over 2 weeks, and positive p-ANCA (anti-MPO) serology.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1520] Renal Cell Carcinoma

**Cluster**: renal cell carcinoma | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) comprises a heterogeneous group of malignancies arising from renal tubular epithelium, predominantly clear cell RCC (75–80%). Treatment paradigms for localized disease prioritize nephron-sparing surgery, while metastatic disease management has been revolutionized by combinations of immune checkpoint inhibitors and VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

### Core Teaching Points
- Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common histological subtype (75-80%), characterized pathologically by loss of chromosome 3p and biallelic inactivation of the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumor suppressor gene, leading to accumulation of hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF-1a/2a) and overexpression of VEGF and PDGF. (PMID 42726211)
- For localized T1 renal tumors (<=7 cm), partial nephrectomy (nephron-sparing surgery) is the preferred standard of care over radical nephrectomy, preserving long-term renal function and reducing cardiovascular mortality with oncological equivalence. (PMID 42604476)
- Active surveillance is an evidence-based management strategy for small renal masses (<3 cm) in elderly or comorbid patients, given the slow median growth rate (approx. 0.1–0.3 cm/year) and very low metastatic potential during initial monitoring. (PMID 42493401)
- For treatment-naive metastatic clear cell RCC, risk-stratified combination therapy based on the IMDC (International Metastatic RCC Database Consortium) criteria is standard: dual immune checkpoint inhibition (nivolumab plus ipilimumab) or ICI-TKI combinations (pembrolizumab plus axitinib, nivolumab plus cabozantinib, or pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib) achieve superior overall survival over sunitinib. (PMID 42779347)
- RCC is historically refractory to cytotoxic chemotherapy and conventional radiotherapy; targeted therapies include multi-targeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (cabozantinib, axitinib), mTOR inhibitors (everolimus), and the first-in-class HIF-2alpha inhibitor belzutifan for VHL-associated RCC. (PMID 42722945)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Role of adjuvant pembrolizumab in intermediate-high risk resected ccRCC balancing disease-free survival benefits against immune-related toxicities (KEYNOTE-564).
- Optimal second-line sequencing following progression on first-line IO-TKI combinations in metastatic clear cell RCC.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Surgical choice for T1a renal mass: partial nephrectomy is strongly preferred over radical nephrectomy to preserve nephron mass and renal function.
- Molecular pathophysiology of clear cell RCC: VHL gene inactivation on chromosome 3p leading to constitutive activation of HIF pathways and hypervascularity.
- First-line systemic therapy for poor/intermediate-risk metastatic ccRCC: combination immunotherapy with nivolumab plus ipilimumab or pembrolizumab plus axitinib/lenvatinib.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 62-year-old man found to have an incidental 3.2-cm solid, enhancing, exophytic mass in the lower pole of the right kidney on an abdominal ultrasound for gallstones.
- A 54-year-old woman presenting with left flank pain, microscopic hematuria, and multiple cannonball pulmonary metastases on chest CT.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1522] Renal Hypertension: Secondary Causes

**Cluster**: renal hypertension secondary causes | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Renal disease is the single most common cause of secondary hypertension, divided into renal parenchymal disease and renovascular hypertension. Identifying renovascular stenosis, particularly in young females (fibromuscular dysplasia) or older atherosclerotic patients, allows targeted medical and interventional management.

### Core Teaching Points
- Renal parenchymal disease causes hypertension through impaired sodium excretion, intravascular volume expansion, and secondary activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS); blood pressure target is <130/80 mmHg using ACE inhibitors or ARBs as first-line therapy to reduce proteinuria and slow CKD progression. (PMID 42812167)
- Renovascular hypertension is caused by renal artery stenosis (RAS), which is divided into atherosclerotic RAS (>90% of cases, typically affecting older males at the ostium/proximal third of the artery) and fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD, ~10%, classically affecting young females aged 15-50 in the mid-to-distal artery with a 'string-of-beads' appearance). (PMID 39465780)
- Clinical clues indicating renovascular hypertension include severe or resistant hypertension, acute elevation of serum creatinine >30% following initiation of an ACE inhibitor or ARB, recurrent unprovoked flash pulmonary edema, an abdominal systolic-diastolic bruit, and asymmetric kidney sizes (>1.5 cm length discrepancy). (PMID 39911662)
- Catheter-based percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) without stenting is the curative treatment of choice for fibromuscular dysplasia, achieving high rates of blood pressure normalization; in contrast, routine stenting for atherosclerotic RAS (ASTRAL and CORAL trials) does not improve blood pressure or renal outcomes over medical therapy alone. (PMID 15312219)
- Initial non-invasive screening for suspected renal artery stenosis utilizes renal duplex ultrasonography (peak systolic velocity >200 cm/s, renal-to-aortic velocity ratio >3.5), CT angiography (avoided in advanced renal impairment), or contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance angiography (MRA). (PMID 42812167)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Compelling criteria for revascularization in atherosclerotic RAS (refractory flash pulmonary edema, rapidly progressive ischemic nephropathy).
- Screening algorithms and diagnostic criteria for non-atherosclerotic renal artery aneurysms and spontaneous renal artery dissections in patients with FMD.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- FMD versus Atherosclerotic RAS: FMD responds curative to percutaneous balloon angioplasty without stenting, whereas atherosclerotic RAS is primarily managed with optimal medical therapy.
- ACE inhibitor hemodynamic effect: acute rise in serum creatinine >30% upon starting ACEi/ARB suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of a solitary functioning kidney.
- Preferred non-invasive screening test: Doppler ultrasonography of renal arteries evaluates hemodynamic velocity shifts without exposing patients to iodinated contrast or gadolinium.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 28-year-old previously healthy woman with newly diagnosed severe hypertension (BP 185/110 mmHg) and an epigastric bruit on physical examination.
- A 72-year-old man with peripheral vascular disease and baseline creatinine 1.4 mg/dL whose creatinine spikes to 2.8 mg/dL 10 days after starting lisinopril 10 mg daily.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1523] Renal Imaging in Nephrology

**Cluster**: renal imaging in nephrology | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Radiological imaging is integral to the diagnosis, staging, and monitoring of kidney disorders. Selecting the appropriate modality—renal ultrasound, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or radionuclide scintigraphy—requires balancing anatomical resolution against potential nephrotoxic and systemic risks.

### Core Teaching Points
- Renal ultrasonography is the first-line imaging modality in nephrology, accurately evaluating kidney size, cortical echogenicity, corticomedullary differentiation, and excluding post-renal obstructive uropathy (hydronephrosis) without radiation exposure or nephrotoxicity. (PMID 41348211)
- Bilateral small (<9 cm), hyperechoic kidneys with thin cortices and poor corticomedullary differentiation indicate irreversible chronic kidney disease; normal or enlarged kidneys in renal failure suggest diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis, polycystic kidney disease, HIV-associated nephropathy, or acute glomerulonephritis. (PMID 41464210)
- Non-contrast low-dose CT of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (CT KUB) is the gold standard imaging modality for suspected nephrolithiasis, boasting >95% sensitivity and specificity and detecting all stone types (including radiolucent uric acid stones) except rare indinavir-induced stones. (PMID 42758233)
- Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) and post-contrast acute kidney injury (PC-AKI) risk with modern low-osmolar or iso-osmolar iodinated contrast is low, but rises in severe CKD (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m2); preventive measures center on volume expansion with isotonic crystalloids (saline), while sodium bicarbonate and N-acetylcysteine are no longer routinely recommended. (PMID 41552567)
- Gadolinium-based contrast agents carry a risk of Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis (NSF) in severe kidney failure (eGFR <15-30 mL/min/1.73m2); modern macrocyclic Class II agents (e.g., gadobutrol, gadoterate) carry negligible risk and can be safely administered when clinically indicated. (PMID 40293518)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Clinical utility of ultrasound shear-wave elastography in quantifying renal cortical interstitial fibrosis non-invasively.
- True incidence of post-contrast acute kidney injury in stable outpatients with eGFR 20-30 mL/min receiving modern iso-osmolar contrast.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Kidney size in chronic renal failure: kidneys are typically shrunken (<9 cm), but enlarged/normal sized in diabetic nephropathy, amyloidosis, and myeloma kidney.
- Imaging test of choice for acute flank pain and suspected ureteric colic: non-contrast CT KUB, which detects stone location, diameter, and secondary signs of obstruction.
- Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis risk profile: high-risk linear gadolinium chelates are contraindicated in severe CKD; macrocyclic Class II agents have an exemplary safety profile.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 48-year-old man presenting with acute severe left flank pain radiating to the groin with microscopic hematuria, evaluated for optimal diagnostic imaging.
- A 65-year-old woman with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m2) requiring an urgent contrast-enhanced CT to stage newly diagnosed colon cancer.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1524] Renal Manifestations of Systemic Disease

**Cluster**: renal manifestations of systemic disease | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
The kidneys are frequently involved in multi-organ systemic disorders including diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic vasculitis, amyloidosis, and multiple myeloma. Recognizing distinct clinical and urinalysis signatures enables early diagnosis and targeted therapy to preserve renal function.

### Core Teaching Points
- Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease worldwide, characterized histologically by glomerular basement membrane thickening, mesangial expansion, and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules); comprehensive therapy incorporates ACEi/ARB, SGLT2 inhibitors, and non-steroidal mineralocorticoid antagonists (finerenone). (PMID 42664148)
- Lupus nephritis affects up to 50% of SLE patients and is classified by ISN/RPS criteria into Classes I through VI; Class III (focal) and Class IV (diffuse proliferative) represent aggressive glomerulonephritides requiring urgent induction immunosuppression with mycophenolate mofetil or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide combined with high-dose corticosteroids. (PMID 38181809)
- Renal amyloidosis (AL and AA) typically manifests as heavy, nephrotic-range proteinuria and progressive renal failure with normal or enlarged kidneys on ultrasound; diagnosis is confirmed by Congo red staining demonstrating apple-green birefringence under polarized light. (PMID 29482993)
- Myeloma kidney (light chain cast nephropathy) presents with acute or subacute kidney injury caused by excessive monoclonal immunoglobulin free light chains precipitating with Tamm-Horsfall protein in distal tubules; diagnosis requires serum free light chain (sFLC) ratio, and dipstick urinalysis is falsely negative for proteinuria as it only detects albumin. (PMID 42769859)
- Systemic sclerosis can cause scleroderma renal crisis (SRC), characterized by abrupt new-onset accelerated hypertension, oliguric acute kidney injury, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, which must be treated immediately with titrated ACE inhibitors (captopril). (PMID 42806593)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Role of dual targeted B-cell therapies (belimumab plus rituximab) in refractory proliferative lupus nephritis.
- Optimal threshold for emergency extracorporeal light chain removal (high-cutoff hemodialysis or plasma exchange) in severe cast nephropathy.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Urinalysis discrepancy in myeloma kidney: routine urine dipstick detects only albumin and will be negative or trace despite massive Bence-Jones proteinuria, requiring 24-hr protein electrophoresis or serum free light chains.
- Scleroderma renal crisis management: emergency ACE inhibitor titration (captopril) is life-saving; corticosteroids are contraindicated as high doses trigger SRC.
- Pathognomonic histology in diabetic nephropathy: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular intercapillary glomerulosclerosis) on PAS and silver stains.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 68-year-old man presenting with acute kidney injury, normocytic anemia, bone pain, hypercalcemia, and a urine dipstick that is completely negative for protein.
- A 36-year-old woman with diffuse systemic sclerosis who presents with new-onset blood pressure 210/120 mmHg, headache, and serum creatinine doubling to 2.4 mg/dL.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1525] Renal Manifestations of Vasculitis

**Cluster**: renal manifestations of vasculitis | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Systemic vasculitis involving the kidneys typically manifests as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), demanding urgent recognition and immunosuppression to prevent end-stage renal disease. ANCA-associated vasculitis and anti-GBM disease represent the most common and destructive etiologies.

### Core Teaching Points
- ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV—granulomatosis with polyangiitis GPA, microscopic polyangiitis MPA, and eosinophilic GPA) typically causes a pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis, characterized serologically by antibodies against proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA / c-ANCA) or myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA / p-ANCA). (PMID 42664148)
- Urgent induction therapy for organ- or life-threatening AAV combines high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids with either rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks or 1,000 mg on days 1 and 15) or intravenous cyclophosphamide; the ADVOCATE trial established that the oral C5a receptor antagonist avacopan can effectively replace high-dose oral prednisone tapers. (PMID 42602030)
- The landmark PEXIVAS trial demonstrated that routine therapeutic plasma exchange (PEX) did not reduce the composite endpoint of all-cause mortality or end-stage renal disease in severe AAV, although plasma exchange remains standard of care for concurrent anti-GBM disease or severe pulmonary hemorrhage. (PMID 41711936)
- Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture disease) is characterized by circulating autoantibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, presenting with severe crescentic glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage; urgent daily plasma exchange combined with cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids must be initiated before oliguria develops. (PMID 42260845)
- Immunofluorescence examination of the renal biopsy is crucial: AAV demonstrates a 'pauci-immune' pattern (scant or absent immunoglobulin/complement staining), whereas anti-GBM disease displays pathognomonic bright linear IgG staining along glomerular capillary walls. (PMID 42756361)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration of rituximab maintenance therapy (2 years vs extended 4-5 years) in PR3-ANCA patients at high risk of late relapse.
- Safety and efficacy of avacopan in patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m2), who were excluded from the pivotal ADVOCATE trial.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- PEXIVAS trial finding: routine plasma exchange does not reduce death or ESKD in ANCA-associated vasculitis, reserving PEX for severe pulmonary hemorrhage or dual ANCA/anti-GBM positivity.
- Immunofluorescence differentiation: linear IgG along capillary walls indicates anti-GBM disease; granular capillary/mesangial deposits indicate immune-complex GN (lupus, cryoglobulinemia); pauci-immune indicates AAV.
- Avacopan mechanism of action: selective oral C5a receptor antagonist that allows elimination or significant reduction of toxic systemic glucocorticoid exposure in AAV induction.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 64-year-old man presenting with malaise, purpuric skin rash, hemoptysis, dark brown urine with red cell casts, and serum creatinine 4.5 mg/dL with positive c-ANCA/PR3 titers.
- A 22-year-old male smoker presenting with sudden-onset hemoptysis, anuric acute kidney injury, and linear IgG deposition on emergent renal biopsy.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1526] Renal Osteodystrophy

**Cluster**: renal osteodystrophy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Renal osteodystrophy refers to the spectrum of bone morphological alterations occurring in chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD). Derangements in calcium, phosphate, FGF23, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and active vitamin D lead to high-turnover bone disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica) or low-turnover states (adynamic bone disease).

### Core Teaching Points
- Chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD) encompasses biochemical abnormalities (calcium, phosphate, PTH, FGF23, vitamin D), skeletal abnormalities (renal osteodystrophy), and vascular/soft-tissue calcification. (PMID 40446949)
- As GFR declines below 60 mL/min/1.73m2, impaired phosphate excretion stimulates osteocytes to secrete Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 (FGF23); FGF23 promotes phosphaturia but downregulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, reducing active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), causing hypocalcemia and driving secondary hyperparathyroidism. (PMID 42081926)
- High-turnover bone disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica) is driven by elevated PTH, characterized by accelerated osteoclastic bone resorption, osteoblastic marrow fibrosis, and classic subperiosteal bone resorption on radial phalanges; treatment involves dietary phosphate restriction, non-calcium phosphate binders, and calcimimetics (cinacalcet) or vitamin D sterols. (PMID 39156357)
- Adynamic bone disease (ABD) is a low-turnover state characterized by markedly suppressed bone formation and resorption, thin osteoid seams, and cellular hypoplasia, classically provoked by over-suppression of PTH (intact PTH <100 pg/mL) from excessive calcium-containing binders, high-dose active vitamin D, or previous aluminum toxicity. (PMID 42214784)
- In dialysis-dependent CKD (G5D), target intact PTH is maintained within 2 to 9 times the upper limit of normal for the specific assay (approx. 130–600 pg/mL), balancing prevention of osteitis fibrosa cystica against adynamic bone disease. (PMID 41309376)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Diagnostic accuracy of bone-specific alkaline phosphatase and serum markers compared to gold-standard tetracycline double-labeled bone biopsy in guiding CKD-MBD therapy.
- Cardiovascular mortality impact of calcimimetic therapy (cinacalcet/etelcalcetide) versus surgical subtotal parathyroidectomy in severe refractory secondary hyperparathyroidism.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Target intact PTH in dialysis (KDIGO guidelines): 2 to 9 times the assay upper limit of normal (~130–600 pg/mL); normal PTH values in dialysis indicate adynamic bone disease.
- Pathophysiological cascade in early CKD: FGF23 elevation is the earliest detectable mineral metabolism change, occurring before overt hyperphosphatemia or hypocalcemia.
- Radiographic sign of severe secondary hyperparathyroidism: subperiosteal bone resorption along the radial aspect of the middle phalanges and 'rugger-jersey' spine appearance.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 54-year-old man on maintenance hemodialysis for 5 years presenting with diffuse bone pain, an intact PTH of 1,250 pg/mL, serum calcium 2.65 mmol/L, and serum phosphate 2.1 mmol/L.
- A 68-year-old woman on peritoneal dialysis on high-dose calcitriol and calcium carbonate whose intact PTH drops to 35 pg/mL, experiencing an atraumatic femoral neck fracture.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1527] Renal Replacement Therapy Modality Choice

**Cluster**: renal replacement therapy modality choice | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Selecting the optimal renal replacement therapy (RRT) modality for end-stage kidney disease requires collaborative shared decision-making. Hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and kidney transplantation offer distinct lifestyle, clinical, and physiological trade-offs.

### Core Teaching Points
- Kidney transplantation (especially preemptive living-donor transplantation) is the definitive gold-standard renal replacement therapy for eligible patients, providing vastly superior long-term survival, reduced cardiovascular morbidity, and improved quality of life compared with chronic dialysis. (PMID 42203644)
- In-center hemodialysis (ICHD) and peritoneal dialysis (PD) demonstrate equivalent 1- to 2-year survival; PD offers greater preservation of residual kidney function, flexibility, independence, and needle-free therapy, while ICHD provides scheduled, clinician-delivered dialysis without patient self-care burden. (PMID 42519780)
- Peritoneal dialysis is contraindicated in patients with severe peritoneal fibrosis, extensive abdominal adhesions, uncorrectable mechanical abdominal wall or diaphragmatic hernias, or inability to perform sterile exchanges (unless assisted by a caregiver). (PMID 42316052)
- Vascular access planning for hemodialysis prioritizes native arteriovenous fistulas (AVF) over prosthetic arteriovenous grafts (AVG) and central venous catheters (CVC); AVFs have superior long-term patency and lower infection and mortality rates, though require 6 to 12 weeks of maturation before cannulation. (PMID 41715948)
- Conservative (non-dialytic) kidney management is a structured, palliative care-aligned therapeutic option for frail, elderly patients with significant multimorbidity and severe functional impairment, in whom starting dialysis does not prolong life or improve symptom control compared with comprehensive medical management. (PMID 32668114)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Survival and technique durability trade-offs of incremental (once- or twice-weekly) hemodialysis in patients with substantial residual kidney function.
- Optimal patient selection criteria for urgent-start peritoneal dialysis versus temporary central venous catheter-based hemodialysis in acute presentation of ESKD.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Vascular access hierarchy: native arteriovenous fistula (AVF, e.g. radiocephalic or brachiocephalic) is preferred over grafts and catheters due to lowest bacteremia and thrombosis rates.
- Preservation of residual renal function: peritoneal dialysis preserves residual GFR and daily urine volume significantly longer than conventional intermittent hemodialysis.
- Conservative kidney management candidacy: elderly patients (>75-80 years) with high comorbidity (Charlson comorbidity index >=8) and severe frailty derive minimal survival benefit from dialysis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 32-year-old active accountant with stage 5 CKD seeking a dialysis modality that allows continued full-time employment and travel while awaiting a deceased-donor kidney transplant.
- An 82-year-old nursing home resident with severe vascular dementia, heart failure, and eGFR 8 mL/min evaluated for shared decision-making regarding conservative care vs dialysis.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1528] Renal replacement therapy timing in acute kidney injury

**Cluster**: renal replacement therapy timing in acute kidney injury | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Determining the optimal timing for initiating renal replacement therapy (RRT) in acute kidney injury (AKI) balances preventing life-threatening uremic complications against avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures in patients who might recover spontaneously. Landmark randomized trials have firmly established that conservative, demand-driven strategies are safe.

### Core Teaching Points
- Multiple landmark multicenter randomized clinical trials (AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU, STARRT-AKI, and AKIKI-2) consistently demonstrate that an accelerated or early RRT strategy in critically ill patients with AKI does not reduce 60- or 90-day mortality compared with a standard, delayed/demand-driven strategy. (PMID 42316052)
- Delayed, demand-driven RRT initiation avoids invasive dialysis catheterization and extracorporeal circulation in approximately 40–50% of AKI patients who recover intrinsic renal function with medical management alone. (PMID 32668114)
- Absolute, conventional emergency indications for immediate RRT initiation ('AEIOU') include: Refractory severe hyperkalemia (K >6.5 mmol/L or with ECG changes), Refractory severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.15-7.20), Refractory fluid overload / pulmonary edema unresponsive to high-dose loop diuretics, and Overt uremic complications (uremic pericarditis, uremic encephalopathy, uremic bleeding). (PMID 30304656)
- In the absence of emergency indications, waiting until persistent Stage 3 AKI or progressive physiological deterioration occurs is safe; however, waiting until severe uremia (BUN >112-140 mg/dL / urea >40-50 mmol/L) develops (as observed in AKIKI-2) carries increased complications and should be avoided. (PMID 42203644)
- Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and intermittent hemodialysis (IHD) demonstrate equivalent patient survival; CRRT is guideline-preferred in hemodynamically unstable critically ill patients and patients with acute brain injury / elevated intracranial pressure. (PMID 42054520)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Utility of the Furosemide Stress Test (FST—urine output <200 mL within 2 hours of a 1.0–1.5 mg/kg furosemide bolus) in identifying patients destined to require RRT.
- Impact of delayed RRT on long-term development of chronic kidney disease and persistent renal functional recovery at 1 year.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Trial evidence on RRT timing: the STARRT-AKI and AKIKI trials confirmed that accelerated/early RRT initiation does NOT improve survival and increases dialysis dependence and adverse events.
- Absolute indications for emergent RRT: refractory hyperkalemia, refractory pulmonary edema, severe refractory metabolic acidosis (pH <7.15), and uremic pericarditis/encephalopathy.
- Hemodynamic stability and modality choice: CRRT is indicated in septic shock and acute liver failure / cerebral edema to minimize rapid fluid shifts and maintain cerebral perfusion pressure.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 62-year-old critically ill man with septic shock on mechanical ventilation who is oliguric for 24 hours with creatinine 3.8 mg/dL, K 4.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, and no pulmonary edema.
- A 55-year-old woman with acute tubular necrosis who develops a distinct pericardial friction rub and confusion on day 4 of admission with blood urea nitrogen 120 mg/dL.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1529] Renal Transplantation: Workup and Donor Selection

**Cluster**: renal transplantation workup and donor selection | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Renal transplantation candidate and donor workup requires rigorous multidisciplinary evaluation to confirm immunological compatibility, identify cardiovascular and infectious risks, and ensure donor safety. Living-donor kidney transplantation provides superior graft and patient longevity.

### Core Teaching Points
- Pre-transplant evaluation for potential recipients focuses on screening for cardiovascular disease (the leading cause of post-transplant mortality), occult malignancy, active systemic infection (TB, hepatitis B/C, HIV, CMV, EBV), and uncorrectable lower urinary tract abnormalities. (PMID 31983666)
- Immunological assessment incorporates ABO blood group typing, HLA typing (HLA-A, -B, -C, -DR, -DQ, -DP), panel reactive antibody (PRA) or calculated PRA (cPRA) to determine sensitization, and donor-specific antibody (DSA) detection via Luminex single-antigen bead assays. (PMID 42866756)
- A prospective negative T-cell and B-cell crossmatch (complement-dependent cytotoxicity [CDC] or flow cytometry crossmatch) is mandatory before deceased-donor kidney transplantation to prevent catastrophic hyperacute rejection mediated by preformed anti-HLA antibodies. (PMID 42318931)
- Living kidney donor evaluation requires comprehensive assessment to ensure donor safety: confirming normal GFR (>90 mL/min/1.73m2), excluding hypertension, proteinuria (<150 mg/24h), diabetes mellitus, nephrolithiasis, and vascular abnormalities on CT renal angiography; long-term lifetime donor ESRD risk remains exceptionally low (<0.5-1%). (PMID 41293797)
- Cardiovascular screening in asymptomatic high-risk recipients (diabetes, age >50, dialysis vintage >2 years) requires non-invasive functional cardiac stress testing (dobutamine stress echocardiography or myocardial perfusion scintigraphy) with coronary angiography indicated for positive tests. (PMID 42803339)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Safety and long-term allograft survival thresholds for accepting expanded-criteria kidneys from donors with acute kidney injury or hepatitis C viremia treated with direct-acting antivirals.
- Optimal desensitization protocols (plasmapheresis, IVIG, and rituximab) for highly sensitized patients with positive donor-specific antibodies in living-donor paired exchange programs.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Hyperacute rejection mechanism: preformed donor-specific anti-HLA Class I or ABO antibodies causing complement activation, endothelial thrombosis, and graft necrosis within minutes; prevented by prospective crossmatching.
- Living donor GFR threshold: living donor candidates must have an age-adjusted measured or estimated GFR >=90 mL/min/1.73m2 and no persistent microalbuminuria or proteinuria.
- Leading cause of death with a functioning graft: ischemic heart disease, necessitating rigorous pre-transplant cardiovascular risk stratification.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 48-year-old man with polycystic kidney disease whose 45-year-old wife volunteers for living kidney donation, evaluated for ABO compatibility and donor-recipient crossmatching.
- A 62-year-old diabetic woman on hemodialysis evaluated for kidney transplant waitlisting who has a history of asymptomatic inferior Q waves on baseline ECG.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.
