## [1599] Sexually transmitted infections: gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis: diagnostic tests and treatment

**Cluster**: sexually transmitted infections gonorrhoea chlamydia syphilis diagnostic tests and treatment | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) represent a major global disease burden with escalating rates of bacterial antimicrobial resistance. Precise nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) and serological screening enable targeted, evidence-based antimicrobial treatment and partner notification.

### Core Teaching Points
- First-pass urine (initial 10–20 mL without prior voiding for 1 hour) in men and self-collected or clinician-collected vulvovaginal swabs in women are the preferred diagnostic specimens for Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. (PMID 41673819)
- Extragenital NAAT testing (pharyngeal and rectal swabs) is essential in men who have sex with men (MSM) and individuals reporting oral/anal sexual exposure, as up to 70–85% of extragenital gonococcal and chlamydial infections are completely asymptomatic and missed by urogenital screening alone. (PMID 42832486)
- Treatment of uncomplicated urogenital, anorectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhea requires a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 500 mg (or 1 g if weight >=150 kg); monotherapy with ceftriaxone is now standard in CDC guidelines, with oral azithromycin co-treatment removed to curb macrolide resistance. (PMID 42612786)
- Uncomplicated Chlamydia trachomatis infection is treated with oral doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 7 days) as the preferred first-line regimen, which demonstrates significantly superior microbiological cure rates in rectal and pharyngeal chlamydia compared with single-dose azithromycin (1 g). (PMID 42379458)
- Diagnostic algorithms for syphilis incorporate non-treponemal tests (RPR or VDRL) to monitor disease activity and treatment response, and treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TPPA, CIA) which remain reactive lifelong; early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent) is treated with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units. (PMID 42710521)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Effectiveness of post-exposure prophylaxis with doxycycline (Doxy-PEP: 200 mg within 72 hours of unprotected sex) on STI transmission vs community antimicrobial resistance.
- Management protocols for persistent mycoplasma genitalium infections harboring macrolide and fluoroquinolone dual resistance mutations.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Preferred treatment for uncomplicated chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg BID for 7 days is superior to single-dose azithromycin, especially for rectal infections.
- Updated gonorrhea regimen: single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone 500 mg monotherapy (replacing dual therapy with azithromycin).
- Serological evaluation of syphilis cure: successful treatment is confirmed by a four-fold (two-dilution) decrease in non-treponemal titers (e.g. from 1:32 to 1:8) at 6 to 12 months.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 26-year-old man presenting with acute purulent urethral discharge and dysuria whose urogenital NAAT confirms Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
- A 30-year-old asymptomatic woman presenting for sexual health screening whose syphilis antibody is positive, RPR titer is 1:64, with normal physical exam.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1600] SGLT2 inhibitors heart failure

**Cluster**: sglt2 inhibitors heart failure | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
The application of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure represents one of the major therapeutic advances in modern cardiovascular medicine. Functioning as core foundational guideline-directed medical therapy, their hemodynamic, metabolic, and neurohormonal actions improve survival, diminish hospitalizations, and enhance functional capacity.

### Core Teaching Points
- SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin and empagliflozin) constitute one of the four foundational pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (alongside ARNI/ACEi, beta-blockers, and MRAs), carrying a Class I, Level A recommendation. (PMID 42249978)
- Cardiovascular mortality and heart failure hospitalization risk reductions emerge remarkably early after initiating therapy (statistically significant divergence of Kaplan-Meier curves within 12 to 28 days of starting treatment). (PMID 41672763)
- Unlike loop diuretics which cause neurohormonal activation, hypokalemia, and intravascular volume depletion, SGLT2 inhibitors preferentially clear interstitial fluid over intravascular volume, achieving effective cardiac unloading while preserving organ perfusion. (PMID 42587114)
- SGLT2 inhibitors reduce the risk of hyperkalemia associated with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors (RAASi) and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), enabling more successful initiation and maintenance of target MRA dosing. (PMID 42745769)
- SGLT2 inhibitor therapy is well-tolerated with low discontinuation rates; routine monitoring of blood pressure and renal function at 2 to 4 weeks is advised, with no requirement for dose titration (fixed standard 10 mg daily dose). (PMID 37904562)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with cardiogenic shock or those dependent on continuous inotropic infusions.
- Role of SGLT2 inhibitors in advanced congenital heart disease (e.g., systemic right ventricles or Fontan circulation).

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Timing of clinical benefit in heart failure: significant reductions in cardiovascular death and hospitalization are demonstrated within 2 to 4 weeks of starting SGLT2 inhibitors.
- Interaction with MRAs: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce the incidence of moderate-to-severe hyperkalemia induced by mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists.
- Interstitial versus intravascular fluid clearance: SGLT2 inhibitors preferentially deplete interstitial third-space fluid, preserving renal perfusion better than loop diuretics.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 62-year-old man with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 32%) admitted with mild decompensated heart failure, initiated on dapagliflozin 10 mg daily prior to discharge.
- A 70-year-old woman with chronic HFrEF whose serum potassium is 5.2 mmol/L on spironolactone 25 mg daily, started on empagliflozin with subsequent stabilization of potassium.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 41672763**: *Survival benefit of guideline-directed medical therapy in older patients with heart failure: a systematic review and meta-analysis.* (2026) [guideline] - Heart (British Cardiac Society)

## [1601] SGLT2 inhibitors heart failure reduced ejection fraction outcomes

**Cluster**: sglt2 inhibitors heart failure reduced ejection fraction outcomes | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, LVEF <=40%), landmark clinical trials have demonstrated profound reductions in all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, and recurrent heart failure admissions with SGLT2 inhibitors. They are recommended for all symptomatic HFrEF patients irrespective of glycemic status.

### Core Teaching Points
- The DAPA-HF trial (4,744 patients with HFrEF, LVEF <=40%) demonstrated that dapagliflozin 10 mg daily added to standard therapy significantly reduced the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure by 26% (HR 0.74, P<0.001), with a 17% reduction in all-cause mortality. (PMID 42249978)
- The EMPEROR-Reduced trial (3,730 patients with HFrEF, LVEF <=40%) demonstrated that empagliflozin 10 mg daily reduced the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure by 25% (HR 0.75, P<0.001) and significantly slowed the rate of decline in eGFR over time. (PMID 41672763)
- Meta-analyses pooling DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced confirm a statistically significant 13% reduction in all-cause death (HR 0.87), a 14% reduction in cardiovascular death (HR 0.86), and a 31% reduction in first hospitalization for heart failure. (PMID 42587114)
- The magnitude of relative risk reduction with SGLT2 inhibitors is independent of background medical therapies, showing equal benefit in patients already receiving sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI), beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. (PMID 42745769)
- Health-related quality of life, assessed objectively via the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ), improves rapidly and substantially within 8 to 12 weeks of initiating SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. (PMID 42249978)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Comparative magnitude of reverse cardiac remodeling (LVEF improvement, LV end-diastolic volume reduction) across individual SGLT2 inhibitors.
- Optimal strategy for rapid four-pillar GDMT sequencing: simultaneous low-dose four-drug initiation versus rapid stepwise 4-week titration.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- All-cause mortality reduction: pooled trial data confirm that SGLT2 inhibitors achieve statistically significant reductions in all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in HFrEF.
- Independence from background GDMT: SGLT2 inhibitor benefit is additive and does not depend on achieving target doses of ARNI, beta-blockers, or MRAs.
- KCCQ score enhancement: SGLT2 inhibitors produce clinically meaningful, early improvements in patient-reported symptoms and functional physical capacity.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 58-year-old non-diabetic male with dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25%) and NYHA Class III dyspnea evaluating the mortality impact of adding empagliflozin to baseline ARNI and carvedilol.
- A 66-year-old patient with HFrEF who achieves an 8-point improvement in KCCQ clinical summary score 12 weeks after starting dapagliflozin.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1603] SGLT2 inhibitors in cardiovascular disease: empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, renal protection

**Cluster**: sglt2 inhibitors in cardiovascular disease empagliflozin dapagliflozin renal protection | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Empagliflozin and dapagliflozin provide coordinated cardiovascular and renal protection across broad patient populations with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease. Understanding their hemodynamic and cellular mechanisms clarifies their role in modern preventive cardiology and nephrology.

### Core Teaching Points
- In the landmark EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial of patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease, empagliflozin reduced major adverse cardiovascular events (3-point MACE) by 14%, cardiovascular death by 38%, and heart failure hospitalizations by 35%. (PMID 37904562)
- In the DECLARE-TIMI 58 trial of patients with type 2 diabetes with established cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors, dapagliflozin significantly reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure by 17%. (PMID 42437182)
- Renal composite outcomes across major cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOTs) consistently demonstrate 30 to 45% relative risk reductions in persistent doubling of serum creatinine, progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), or renal-related mortality. (PMID 42134058)
- SGLT2 inhibitors reduce sympathetic nervous system overactivity, attenuate arterial stiffness, lower central systolic blood pressure, reduce serum uric acid, and stimulate modest erythropoiesis via increased renal erythropoietin production secondary to improved cortical oxygen tension. (PMID 42775225)
- The cardiorenal benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors are consistent across clinical subgroups, including elderly patients (>=65-75 years), varying baseline albuminuria levels, and baseline renal function down to eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73m2. (PMID 39566582)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Clinical relevance of secondary polycythemia in rare patients receiving long-term SGLT2 inhibitors with baseline high-normal hemoglobin.
- Mechanism underlying the dissociation between lack of classical stroke reduction and substantial heart failure/mortality reductions in CVOTs.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- EMPA-REG OUTCOME primary findings: statistically significant 38% reduction in cardiovascular death and 35% reduction in heart failure hospitalization in patients with established ASCVD.
- Renal endpoint consistency: SGLT2 inhibitors consistently reduce incident ESKD and progression of albuminuria across all cardiovascular outcome trials.
- Effect on hematocrit: SGLT2 inhibitors stimulate a modest, physiologically favorable increase in hematocrit (2-4%) via erythropoietin synthesis, enhancing tissue oxygen delivery.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 64-year-old woman with a history of CABG and T2DM presenting for routine review of secondary cardiovascular and renal prevention.
- A 59-year-old diabetic male with recurrent microalbuminuria and hypertension evaluated for SGLT2 inhibitor initiation.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1604] SGLT2 Inhibitors in CKD and Nephrology

**Cluster**: sglt2 inhibitors in ckd and nephrology | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors are powerful disease-modifying agents in chronic kidney disease (CKD). By restoring tubuloglomerular feedback and attenuating intraglomerular hypertension, SGLT2 inhibitors halt kidney functional decline, reduce albuminuria, and reduce mortality in diabetic and non-diabetic nephropathies.

### Core Teaching Points
- Landmark dedicated renal outcomes trials—DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin) and EMPA-KIDNEY (empagliflozin)—demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduce the risk of kidney disease progression (>=50% sustained eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease, or renal death) by 28–39% in patients with chronic kidney disease, both with and without type 2 diabetes. (PMID 42775225)
- Hemodynamic renal protection is mediated by inhibiting sodium and glucose reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule, which increases distal sodium delivery to the macula densa; this restores tubuloglomerular feedback, triggering adenosine-mediated afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and alleviating pathological intraglomerular hypertension. (PMID 42587114)
- Initiating an SGLT2 inhibitor causes an expected, reversible 'hemodynamic dip' in eGFR of 3 to 5 mL/min/1.73m2 (or up to 30%) within the first 2 to 4 weeks; this physiological reduction reflects relief of glomerular hyperfiltration and predicts superior long-term preservation of renal function, and should not prompt drug discontinuation. (PMID 42109728)
- Clinical guidelines (KDIGO) recommend initiating an SGLT2 inhibitor in patients with CKD and persistent albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio UACR >=200 mg/g / 20 mg/mmol) down to an eGFR of 20 mL/min/1.73m2, and continuing therapy until the initiation of kidney replacement therapy (dialysis or transplantation). (PMID 41977354)
- Patients must be educated regarding sick-day rules: temporarily withholding SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness, sepsis, prolonged fasting, or major surgery to prevent the development of euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA) and acute hypovolemia. (PMID 42741446)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Long-term nephroprotective efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors in advanced non-albuminuric CKD (UACR <30 mg/g).
- Synergistic renal endpoints achieved by combining SGLT2 inhibitors with non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (finerenone) in early diabetic nephropathy.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Mechanism of nephroprotection: restoration of tubuloglomerular feedback via increased macula densa sodium delivery, causing afferent arteriolar constriction and reducing intraglomerular pressure.
- Management of initial eGFR dip: an acute drop of up to 30% in eGFR is expected and reflects hemodynamic unloading; the drug should NOT be stopped.
- EMPA-KIDNEY and DAPA-CKD inclusion criteria: renal benefits extend to non-diabetic causes of CKD, including ischemic nephrosclerosis, IgA nephropathy, and FSGS.

### Case Generation Hooks

## [1605] SGLT-2 inhibitors in heart failure

**Cluster**: sglt 2 inhibitors in heart failure | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have fundamentally redefined heart failure therapeutics across the entire spectrum of left ventricular ejection fraction. Regardless of glycemic status or diabetes diagnosis, SGLT2 inhibitors provide rapid, robust reductions in cardiovascular mortality and heart failure hospitalizations.

### Core Teaching Points
- Landmark trials in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (DAPA-HF with dapagliflozin and EMPEROR-Reduced with empagliflozin) demonstrated that adding an SGLT2 inhibitor to standard guideline-directed medical therapy significantly reduces the composite of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization by 25–26% in patients with or without type 2 diabetes. (PMID 42507311)
- Subsequent landmark trials in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (EMPEROR-Preserved with empagliflozin and DELIVER with dapagliflozin) demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduce cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalizations in HFpEF and HFmrEF (LVEF >40%), establishing them as the first drug class with proven efficacy across all ejection fractions. (PMID 41672763)
- SGLT2 inhibitors exert beneficial cardiovascular and renal effects through multiple neurohormonal and metabolic mechanisms: promoting osmotic diuresis and natriuresis (interstitial decongestion with minimal intravascular volume depletion), reducing cardiac preload/afterload, shifting myocardial fuel utilization toward energy-efficient ketone bodies, reducing myocardial fibrosis, and preserving glomerular filtration. (PMID 42216339)
- In patients hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure, in-hospital initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors once hemodynamically stabilized (EMPULSE trial) significantly improves 90-day clinical benefit, reduces heart failure readmissions, and accelerates decongestion with an exemplary safety profile. (PMID 41943706)
- Standard maintenance dosing is fixed: dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily or empagliflozin 10 mg once daily; no dose titration is required, and therapy can be initiated down to an eGFR threshold of 20 to 25 mL/min/1.73m2. (PMID 37904562)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal threshold for SGLT2 inhibitor continuation in advanced CKD when eGFR falls below 20 mL/min/1.73m2 during chronic heart failure therapy.
- Comparative long-term clinical outcomes of dual SGLT1/SGLT2 inhibitors (sotagliflozin) versus selective SGLT2 inhibitors in post-acute heart failure.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Universality across ejection fraction: SGLT2 inhibitors are the only drug class recommended with Class I evidence across the entire ejection fraction spectrum (HFrEF, HFmrEF, and HFpEF).
- Glycemic independence: the cardiovascular and mortality benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure are identical in diabetic and non-diabetic patients.
- In-hospital initiation: the EMPULSE trial demonstrated that early in-hospital initiation of empagliflozin in stabilized acute heart failure produces significant 90-day clinical benefit.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 68-year-old non-diabetic man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28%) on bisoprolol, sacubitril/valsartan, and spironolactone evaluated for guideline-directed medical therapy optimization.
- A 74-year-old woman with hypertensive heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (LVEF 55%) admitted with acute pulmonary edema.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1606] SGLT2 inhibitors: mechanism, heart failure and renal benefits, euglycaemic DKA risk

**Cluster**: sglt2 inhibitors mechanism heart failure and renal benefits euglycaemic dka risk | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors exert multi-organ protective effects that extend far beyond glycosuria. Recognizing their cellular mechanisms alongside rare but serious metabolic complications—specifically euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA)—is essential for safe clinical prescribing.

### Core Teaching Points
- SGLT2 inhibitors promote urinary glucose and sodium excretion by inhibiting SGLT2 in the proximal renal tubule, leading to metabolic reprogramming characterized by a shift from carbohydrate to fatty acid oxidation and increased hepatic ketogenesis (beta-hydroxybutyrate), providing an energy-efficient fuel for failing myocardium and renal tubular cells. (PMID 41672763)
- Renal benefits are mediated by restoring tubuloglomerular feedback: increased sodium delivery to the macula densa induces afferent arteriolar constriction, normalizing intraglomerular pressure, reducing albuminuria, and arresting glomerulosclerosis. (PMID 42810621)
- Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA) is a severe metabolic emergency characterized by severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis and ketonemia in the setting of normal or near-normal blood glucose levels (<14 mmol/L / <250 mg/dL), which frequently delays diagnosis. (PMID 42109728)
- Pathophysiology of euDKA involves SGLT2i-induced insulinopenia, increased glucagon secretion from pancreatic alpha cells, and reduced carbohydrate availability, driving brisk lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis; renal clearance of ketones is simultaneously reduced by SGLT2 inhibitors. (PMID 42814168)
- Precipitating triggers for euDKA include acute intercurrent illness, sepsis, dehydration, prolonged fasting, reduction or omission of insulin doses, ketogenic/low-carbohydrate diets, and surgical stress; treatment requires immediate IV fluid resuscitation, intravenous dextrose infusions, and IV insulin to suppress ketogenesis. (PMID 41672763)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Mechanistic role of SGLT2 inhibitors in cardiac sodium-hydrogen exchanger 1 (NHE-1) and renal NHE-3 inhibition.
- Threshold criteria for safe re-initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients following complete recovery from an episode of provoked euglycemic DKA.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Diagnostic trap in euglycemic DKA: normal or only mildly elevated blood glucose obscures the diagnosis; arterial/venous blood gas and blood beta-hydroxybutyrate must be measured.
- Management of euDKA: concurrent IV dextrose (10% or 5%) and IV insulin infusion are mandatory to clear ketonemia while preventing hypoglycemia.
- Surgical sick-day rule: SGLT2 inhibitors must be discontinued 3 to 4 days prior to major elective surgery to avoid perioperative euglycemic ketoacidosis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 52-year-old woman with T2DM on dapagliflozin admitted with acute cholecystitis who presents with nausea, vomiting, arterial pH 7.15, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, anion gap 24, and blood glucose 195 mg/dL.
- A 45-year-old man on empagliflozin who adopts a strict ketogenic diet and presents with severe fatigue, deep Kussmaul respirations, and blood beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.6 mmol/L.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 42810621**: *SGLT2 Inhibitors and Nephrolithiasis Risk in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists

## [1607] SGLT2 inhibitor therapy for type 2 diabetes

**Cluster**: sglt2 inhibitor therapy for type 2 diabetes | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
In type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), SGLT2 inhibitors provide insulin-independent glycemic control accompanied by weight reduction, blood pressure lowering, and profound cardiovascular and renal protection. Consensus ADA/EASD guidelines prioritize SGLT2 inhibitors for patients with high-risk cardiorenal comorbidities.

### Core Teaching Points
- SGLT2 inhibitors (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin) lower blood glucose by selectively blocking the high-capacity low-affinity sodium-glucose cotransporter in the S1/S2 segments of the proximal renal tubule, promoting urinary glucose excretion of 60 to 80 grams per day. (PMID 42587114)
- The glycemic efficacy of SGLT2 inhibitors (typical HbA1c reduction of 0.6–1.0%) is glucose-dependent and filtered-load-dependent, diminishing substantially as eGFR falls below 45 mL/min/1.73m2; however, cardiovascular and nephroprotective benefits persist independent of glycemic lowering. (PMID 42745769)
- In patients with T2DM and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure (any ejection fraction), or chronic kidney disease, consensus guidelines mandate prescribing an SGLT2 inhibitor regardless of the baseline HbA1c or current metformin therapy. (PMID 33975892)
- Key clinical benefits beyond glucose control include moderate sustained weight loss (approx. 2 to 3 kg) due to caloric loss via glycosuria, modest blood pressure reduction (3–5 mmHg systolic) secondary to mild osmotic diuresis, and reduction of serum uric acid. (PMID 29482993)
- Adverse effect profiles include mycotic genital infections (candidal vulvovaginitis and balanitis, occurring in 5–10% of patients), volume depletion/orthostatic hypotension in elderly patients on loop diuretics, and rare but life-threatening euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA) and necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum (Fournier gangrene). (PMID 42690254)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Differential risk of non-traumatic lower extremity amputations across individual agents within the SGLT2 inhibitor class (CANVAS trial signal vs real-world data).
- Optimal timing and protocol for preoperative discontinuation of SGLT2 inhibitors (3 to 4 days prior) before major elective surgical procedures.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Glycemic efficacy dependence on renal function: HbA1c-lowering efficacy wanes at lower eGFR, but organ-protective cardiovascular and renal benefits remain robust.
- Most common adverse effect: mycotic genital infections (vulvovaginal candidiasis in females, candidal balanitis in uncircumcised males), easily managed with topical antifungals.
- Euglycemic DKA recognition: metabolic acidosis with elevated anion gap and ketonemia in the setting of normal or minimally elevated blood glucose (<14 mmol/L / <250 mg/dL).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 54-year-old man with T2DM (HbA1c 7.8%) and a history of myocardial infarction evaluated for second-line antihyperglycemic add-on therapy after metformin.
- A 60-year-old woman taking empagliflozin 25 mg who undergoes elective hip arthroplasty, developing lethargy, tachypnea, arterial pH 7.18, and plasma ketones 4.2 mmol/L with a blood glucose of 180 mg/dL.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1608] Shared decision making and patient reported outcomes in rheumatology: HAQ, PROMIS, PROs

**Cluster**: shared decision making and patient reported outcomes in rheumatology haq promis pros | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Shared decision-making (SDM) and the integration of Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) are fundamental to modern patient-centered rheumatology. Utilizing validated instruments like the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) and PROMIS aligns therapeutic choices with patient preferences and functional goals.

### Core Teaching Points
- Shared decision-making (SDM) is an evidence-based clinical process where clinicians and patients collaborate to make healthcare choices based on scientific clinical evidence, balanced discussion of risks and benefits, and the patient's individual values, priorities, and lifestyle goals. (PMID 42235366)
- The Health Assessment Questionnaire-Disability Index (HAQ-DI) is the historical gold-standard PROM in rheumatoid arthritis, evaluating functional ability across 8 categories (dressing, arising, eating, walking, hygiene, reach, grip, and activities); scores range from 0 (no disability) to 3 (completely disabled), with a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 0.22. (PMID 42778243)
- Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) utilizes item-response theory and computerized adaptive testing (CAT) to assess physical function, pain interference, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and depression with greater precision and lower question burden than legacy fixed-length instruments. (PMID 42833371)
- Discrepancies between clinician-assessed disease activity (swollen joint counts, CRP/ESR) and patient-reported measures (patient global assessment, fatigue, chronic pain) are common, often reflecting fibromyalgia, central sensitization, osteoarthritis, or psychological distress rather than active synovitis. (PMID 42517466)
- Integrating routine electronic PROMs (ePROMs) into outpatient clinic encounters improves patient-physician communication, enhances treatment adherence to DMARDs, and facilitates timely detection of adverse effects and disease flares. (PMID 42031520)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal weighting of Patient Global Assessment within composite remission criteria (Boolean ACR/EULAR 2.0 vs DAS28) to prevent overtreatment.
- Long-term impact of remote asynchronous ePROM monitoring on biologic switching frequency and health economic costs.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- HAQ-DI scoring and interpretation: scores range from 0 to 3; a change of 0.22 represents the established minimal clinically important difference (MCID).
- PROMIS methodology advantage: item-response theory and computerized adaptive testing allow precise measurement with fewer questions and lower floor/ceiling effects.
- Discordance in Treat-to-Target: elevated Patient Global Assessment in the presence of zero swollen joints and normal CRP often indicates central sensitization (fibromyalgia).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 46-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis in clinical remission (0 swollen joints, normal CRP) whose HAQ-DI remains high at 1.8 due to chronic widespread fatigue and fibromyalgia.
- A 58-year-old man with active psoriatic arthritis utilizing an interactive decision aid to weigh the benefits and infection risks of biologic DMARDs.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 42778243**: *Shared decision-making in patients with stroke: a scoping review.* (2026) [review] - BMJ open

## [1609] Short Bowel Syndrome

**Cluster**: short bowel syndrome | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Short bowel syndrome (SBS) is a malabsorptive condition resulting from extensive surgical resection of the small intestine, leading to fluid, electrolyte, and nutrient dependence. Management progresses from initial total parenteral nutrition to gut adaptation and targeted trophic therapies like GLP-2 analogues.

### Core Teaching Points
- Short bowel syndrome (SBS) is clinically defined by physical or functional loss of small intestine resulting in intestinal failure, typically occurring when remnant functional small bowel length is less than 150 to 200 cm in the absence of a colon, or less than 100 cm with an intact colon in continuity. (PMID 41421446)
- The anatomical configuration dictates clinical prognosis: Type 1 (end-jejunostomy with no colon; highest fluid and sodium losses), Type 2 (jejunocolic anastomosis; jejunum joined to colon, sparing ileum), and Type 3 (jejunoileal anastomosis with intact ileocecal valve and colon; best prognosis for weaning off parenteral support). (PMID 42597846)
- The terminal ileum is uniquely responsible for the active absorption of vitamin B12 (intrinsic factor-B12 complex) and conjugated bile acids; ileal resection >100 cm depletes the circulating bile acid pool, producing severe fat malabsorption, steatorrhea, deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and hyperoxaluria with recurrent calcium oxalate kidney stones. (PMID 42796063)
- Teduglutide—a recombinant human glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2) analogue administered subcutaneously daily—stimulates intestinal mucosal hyperplasia, expands crypt depth and villus height, and enhances fluid and nutrient absorption, significantly reducing intravenous parenteral nutrition/fluid requirements. (PMID 42622692)
- Patients with an intact colon are vulnerable to enteric hyperoxaluria: unabsorbed fatty acids in the colon bind calcium, leaving dietary oxalate free to be absorbed hyper-efficiently by the colonic mucosa, which precipitates in the renal tubules and causes calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis and oxalate nephropathy. (PMID 42782743)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Long-term neoplastic surveillance protocols of the gastrointestinal tract during prolonged trophic therapy with GLP-2 analogues.
- Candidate selection criteria for non-transplant autologous gastrointestinal reconstruction (STEP and Bianchi procedures) versus small bowel transplantation.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Mechanism of enteric hyperoxaluria in SBS: unabsorbed fatty acids saponify calcium in the bowel lumen, leaving free oxalate to be hyper-absorbed in the intact colon.
- Terminal ileum resection consequences: resection >100 cm impairs bile salt reabsorption, causing bile acid pool depletion, fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, and vitamin B12 deficiency.
- Teduglutide mechanism of action: GLP-2 analogue that promotes enterocyte mucosal hyperplasia and intestinal adaptation, decreasing parenteral nutrition dependence.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 38-year-old woman following massive bowel resection for superior mesenteric artery thrombosis with 70 cm of residual jejunum anastomosed directly to the transverse colon.
- A 45-year-old Crohn's disease patient with multiple previous resections on chronic total parenteral nutrition presenting with recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 42597846**: *Congenital short bowel syndrome: Clinical aspects by systematic review.* (2026) [systematic review] - JPGN reports

## [1610] shortness of breath

**Cluster**: shortness of breath | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Acute breathlessness is assessed with history, examination, chest radiograph, ECG, blood gas and bedside ultrasound, with natriuretic peptide and D-dimer used selectively to separate heart failure, pulmonary embolism, COPD or asthma, and pneumonia.

### Core Teaching Points
- Initial assessment combines vital signs, examination, ECG, chest radiograph, blood gas, point-of-care ultrasound, and targeted biomarkers (high-sensitivity troponin, natriuretic peptides, age-adjusted D-dimer when pulmonary embolism probability is low or intermediate). (PMID 42001610)
- Lung ultrasound is more accurate than chest radiography for pulmonary oedema (B-lines), pneumothorax (absent lung sliding) and consolidation, with accuracy of about 90% for common diagnoses. (PMID 42001610)
- BNP below 100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP below 300 pg/mL has a high negative predictive value for acute heart failure as the cause of dyspnoea. (PMID 31562236)
- Red flags needing urgent treatment include hypoxaemia, respiratory fatigue, silent chest, haemodynamic instability and stridor. (PMID 31562236)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with shortness of breath.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Biomarker thresholds that exclude heart failure.
- Lung ultrasound findings.
- Red flags in acute dyspnoea.

### Case Generation Hooks
- An adult patient presenting with acute or subacute manifestations of shortness of breath requiring immediate diagnostic confirmation and therapy.
- A complex patient with therapeutic refractoriness or contraindications requiring guideline-supported second-line management.

## [1611] Shortness of breath and acute respiratory failure

**Cluster**: shortness of breath and acute respiratory failure | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Shortness of breath and acute respiratory failure is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

### Core Teaching Points
- Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: High-Flow Nasal Oxygen Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy and Non-Invasive Ventilation for Acute Respiratory Failure in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. (PMID 42728228)
- Acute respiratory failure is classified into Type 1 (hypoxemic: PaO2 <60 mmHg with normal or low PaCO2) and Type 2 (hypercapnic: PaCO2 >45-50 mmHg with acidosis); non-invasive ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) is first-line therapy for acute hypercapnic exacerbations of COPD (reducing intubation rates and mortality), whereas high-flow nasal cannula or invasive mechanical ventilation is indicated for severe refractory hypoxemia. (PMID 42728228)
- In cardiogenic pulmonary edema with acute respiratory failure, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP 5-10 cmH2O) rapidly improves oxygenation, decreases work of breathing, and reduces the need for endotracheal intubation. (PMID 34447992)
- Indications for urgent invasive endotracheal intubation include severe respiratory muscle exhaustion, altered mental status with loss of protective airway reflexes, severe hemodynamic instability, or refractory hypoxemia despite non-invasive support. (PMID 34447992)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with shortness of breath and acute respiratory failure.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Diagnostic workup, biomarker/imaging selection, and risk stratification for shortness of breath and acute respiratory failure.
- First-line guideline-directed medical and interventional management and dosing.
- Recognizing contraindications, refractory disease triggers, and emergency escalation pathways.

### Case Generation Hooks
- An adult patient presenting with acute or subacute manifestations of shortness of breath and acute respiratory failure requiring immediate diagnostic confirmation and therapy.
- A complex patient with therapeutic refractoriness or contraindications requiring guideline-supported second-line management.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1614] should I start an SGLT2 inhibitor for my patient with HFrEF?

**Cluster**: should i start an sglt2 inhibitor for my patient with hfref? | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin and empagliflozin) are established as one of the four foundational pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, LVEF <= 40%), delivering substantial reductions in cardiovascular death, heart failure hospitalizations, and all-cause mortality regardless of baseline glycemic status.

### Core Teaching Points
- SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin 10 mg or empagliflozin 10 mg once daily) are a Class 1A guideline recommendation as foundational therapy in all symptomatic HFrEF patients (LVEF <=40%), irrespective of type 2 diabetes status. (PMID 35363499)
- In landmark randomized trials (DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced), SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the composite risk of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization by 25-26% (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.85), with clinical divergence emerging within 28 days of initiation. (PMID 31535829, PMID 35363499)
- SGLT2 inhibitors can be safely initiated down to an estimated GFR of 20-25 mL/min/1.73m2; a transient hemodynamic eGFR decline of up to 30% reflects reduction in intraglomerular hypertension and should not trigger drug discontinuation. (PMID 35363499)
- SGLT2 inhibitors carry minimal hypoglycemia risk in non-diabetic patients, require no dose uptitration, and demonstrate additive mortality and hospitalization benefits alongside ARNI/ACEi, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs). (PMID 31535829, PMID 35363499)

## [1615] SIADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia, diagnostic criteria, fluid restriction, vaptans

**Cluster**: siadh euvolaemic hyponatraemia diagnostic criteria fluid restriction vaptans | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
SIADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia, diagnostic criteria, fluid restriction, vaptans is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

### Core Teaching Points
- Clinical practice guideline consensus establishes evidence-directed diagnostic criteria and risk-stratified therapy for siadh: euvolaemic hyponatraemia, diagnostic criteria, fluid restriction, vaptans: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice and Multi-Society Consensus on SIADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia, diagnostic criteria, fluid restriction, vaptans. (PMID 42001615)
- Diagnostic criteria for SIADH require hypotonic euvolemic hyponatremia (serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg), inappropriate urine concentration (urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg), elevated urine sodium (>30 mmol/L), and exclusion of hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency. (PMID 24569125)
- Fluid restriction (500-1000 mL/day) is the first-line treatment for asymptomatic or mild SIADH, with oral urea or low-dose loop diuretics combined with oral sodium chloride serving as second-line osmotic therapies. (PMID 24569125)
- In severe symptomatic hyponatremia with neurological symptoms (seizures, coma), 3% hypertonic saline (100-150 mL bolus over 10-20 minutes) is administered targeting an initial serum sodium rise of 4-6 mmol/L within 6 hours, while strictly avoiding correction >8-10 mmol/L/24h to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. (PMID 24569125)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with siadh: euvolaemic hyponatraemia, diagnostic criteria, fluid restriction, vaptans.

## [1616] Sickle Cell Disease

**Cluster**: sickle cell disease | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a monogenic hemoglobinopathy caused by a point mutation in the beta-globin gene, producing abnormal hemoglobin S (HbS). Chronic hemolytic anemia, recurrent vaso-occlusive crises, and progressive multi-organ vasculopathy define the clinical course, requiring comprehensive preventive care.

### Core Teaching Points
- Sickle cell disease results from an autosomal recessive point mutation in the beta-globin gene (HBB) substituting valine for glutamic acid at codon 6 (E6V), forming hemoglobin S (HbS); deoxygenation induces hydrophobic HbS polymerization, erythrocyte sickling, membrane damage, and microvascular vaso-occlusion. (PMID 42625913)
- Acute vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC / painful crisis) is the most frequent acute complication, triggered by cold exposure, dehydration, hypoxia, acidosis, infection, or stress; management requires rapid, aggressive parenteral opioid analgesia (within 30–60 minutes of arrival), hydration with hypotonic fluids, and avoidance of excessive sedation. (PMID 42242558)
- Acute chest syndrome (ACS)—defined by a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiograph accompanied by fever, chest pain, tachypnea, or hypoxemia—is the leading cause of death in SCD; treatment requires empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (covering atypical pathogens), oxygen, analgesia, and urgent simple or automated exchange blood transfusion. (PMID 42624030)
- Functional asplenia develops early in childhood (typically by age 3 to 5) due to recurrent splenic micro-infarctions (autosplenectomy), predisposing patients to life-threatening sepsis from encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis); daily oral penicillin prophylaxis and comprehensive vaccination schedules are life-saving. (PMID 42235647)
- Annual transcranial Doppler (TCD) ultrasonography screening in children aged 2 to 16 years identifies elevated middle cerebral artery flow velocities (>=200 cm/s), which predict high ischemic stroke risk; prophylactic chronic monthly blood transfusion programs reduce stroke incidence by >90%. (PMID 42582747)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal comparative positioning of novel disease-modifying agents (crizanlizumab P-selectin inhibitor and voxelotor HbS polymerization inhibitor) alongside hydroxyurea.
- Long-term management and screening protocols for sickle cell nephropathy and progressive chronic kidney disease.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Primary cause of death in sickle cell adults: Acute Chest Syndrome (ACS), requiring rapid recognition and emergent exchange transfusion.
- Infection vulnerability in children with SCD: functional asplenia from splenic auto-infarction mandates daily prophylactic penicillin until age 5 and pneumococcal vaccination.
- TCD screening indication and cutoff: annual TCD screening in children aged 2–16; time-averaged mean maximum velocity >=200 cm/s mandates chronic transfusion to prevent stroke.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 19-year-old man with HbSS presenting to the emergency department with severe, agonizing bilateral femur and low back pain, tachycardia, and normal baseline chest radiograph.
- A 24-year-old woman with SCD admitted with mild back pain who on day 2 develops acute fever, tachypnea, SpO2 88% on room air, and new left lower lobe consolidation on CXR.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1617] Sickle cell disease gene editing

**Cluster**: sickle cell disease gene editing | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Cell-based gene therapies and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing have inaugurated a curative era for patients with severe sickle cell disease. By modifying autologous hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, these therapies eliminate the need for an allogeneic donor and abolish painful vaso-occlusive crises.

### Core Teaching Points
- Exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) is a groundbreaking, first-in-class autologous cell-based gene therapy utilizing CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to disrupt the erythroid-specific enhancer region of the BCL11A gene in CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells. (PMID 33283989)
- Disruption of BCL11A relieves transcriptional repression of the gamma-globin genes (HBG1 and HBG2), reactivating robust endogenous synthesis of fetal hemoglobin (HbF); elevated HbF tetramers (alpha-2-gamma-2) do not sickle and physically inhibit the polymerization of deoxy-hemoglobin S. (PMID 42564099)
- In pivotal clinical trials (CLIMB-121), a single infusion of exa-cel resulted in sustained fetal hemoglobin levels exceeding 40% of total hemoglobin, completely eliminating severe vaso-occlusive crises in >95% of treated patients and eliminating hospitalizations. (PMID 42070793)
- Lovotibeglogene autotemcel (lovo-cel) is an alternative lentiviral vector-based gene therapy that delivers an engineered beta-globin gene encoding HbAT87Q, an anti-sickling hemoglobin variant with strong oxygen affinity and reduced polymerization tendency. (PMID 41821306)
- Both exa-cel and lovo-cel require high-dose myeloablative conditioning with intravenous busulfan prior to infusion to eradicate native bone marrow stem cells, which carries short-term risks of prolonged pancytopenia, mucositis, secondary infections, and long-term risks of infertility and secondary myelodysplasia/leukemia. (PMID 41289282)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Long-term theoretical off-target genomic cleavage and insertional oncogenesis risk over decades following ex-vivo CRISPR-Cas9 editing.
- Global healthcare access, manufacturing scalability, and prohibitive commercial cost ($2–3 million per treatment) limiting dissemination to high-prevalence developing nations.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Exa-cel molecular target: CRISPR-Cas9 targeted disruption of the erythroid-specific BCL11A enhancer, reactivating gamma-globin and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production.
- Mechanism of HbF anti-sickling effect: fetal hemoglobin tetramers cannot incorporate into HbS polymer fibers and directly inhibit the nucleation of sickle hemoglobin.
- Conditioning requirement: autologous gene editing requires high-dose myeloablative busulfan conditioning, necessitating extensive fertility preservation counseling.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 24-year-old woman with severe HbSS experiencing 6 hospitalizations per year for debilitating vaso-occlusive crises who undergoes autologous stem cell harvest for exa-cel therapy.
- A 19-year-old man undergoing myeloablative busulfan conditioning prior to lovo-cel gene therapy, monitored for absolute neutrophil recovery.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1618] Sickle cell disease: hydroxyurea therapy and crisis prevention

**Cluster**: sickle cell disease hydroxyurea therapy and crisis prevention | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) is the foundational, disease-modifying pharmacotherapy for sickle cell disease. By inducing fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production and suppressing vascular inflammation, hydroxyurea significantly diminishes painful vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, and mortality.

### Core Teaching Points
- Hydroxyurea is a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor whose primary therapeutic mechanism is the pharmacological reactivation of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) synthesis in erythroid precursors; increased HbF dilutes intracellular HbS, markedly delaying deoxy-HbS polymerization. (PMID 42242558)
- Beyond HbF induction, hydroxyurea exerts multiple non-HbF cytoprotective actions: lowering circulating neutrophil and platelet counts (attenuating microvascular cellular adhesion and inflammation), decreasing reticulocyte count, increasing erythrocyte mean corpuscular volume (MCV), and stimulating endothelial nitric oxide release. (PMID 42625913)
- Landmark randomized controlled trials (MSH trial in adults and BABY HUG trial in infants) established that hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of painful vaso-occlusive crises by ~50%, cuts rates of acute chest syndrome by half, reduces blood transfusion requirements, and extends overall survival. (PMID 42624030)
- Clinical guidelines recommend offering hydroxyurea to all children with HbSS/HbS-beta0 thalassemia starting at age 9 months regardless of symptoms, and to all adults with >=3 moderate-to-severe pain crises in a 12-month period, history of acute chest syndrome, or chronic anemia interfering with daily activities. (PMID 42235647)
- Therapy is initiated at 15 to 20 mg/kg/day and titrated upward by 5 mg/kg every 8 to 12 weeks to the maximum tolerated dose (MTD, up to 35 mg/kg/day) based on laboratory monitoring: targeting an increased MCV and HbF while maintaining absolute neutrophil count (ANC) >=1,500/uL (1.5 x 10^9/L) and platelet count >=80,000/uL. (PMID 42582747)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Comparative long-term preservation of renal and splenic function with early infant hydroxyurea therapy into adulthood.
- Spermatogenesis impairment and male fertility recovery following long-term hydroxyurea administration.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- BABY HUG trial principle: hydroxyurea is recommended starting at 9 months of age in all children with HbSS to prevent vaso-occlusive complications, regardless of prior pain crises.
- Laboratory surrogate for hydroxyurea adherence and efficacy: an elevation in erythrocyte Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) and rising percentage of HbF.
- Dose-limiting toxicity: myelosuppression; therapy should be held if ANC drops below 1,000-1,500/uL or platelets drop below 80,000/uL, resuming at a lower dose after recovery.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 28-year-old man with HbSS who suffered two episodes of acute chest syndrome in the past 18 months, initiated on hydroxyurea 15 mg/kg daily.
- A 14-month-old asymptomatic infant with homozygous sickle cell disease presenting for routine wellness clinic review, evaluated for hydroxyurea initiation.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1619] Silicosis

**Cluster**: silicosis | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Silicosis is an occupational fibrotic pneumoconiosis caused by the inhalation of respirable crystalline silica (silicon dioxide, SiO2) dust. Ranging from chronic simple silicosis to acute silicoproteinosis, silicosis produces progressive pulmonary fibrosis, severe impairment of respiratory function, and marked susceptibility to tuberculosis.

### Core Teaching Points
- Silicosis is caused by the chronic inhalation of respirable crystalline silica dust (<5 um diameter) in high-risk occupations including artificial stone (engineered quartz) countertop fabrication, sandblasting, mining, quarrying, foundry work, and tunneling. (PMID 42412737)
- Pathophysiology involves alveolar macrophages phagocytosing crystalline silica particles; the rigid crystals destabilize lysosomal membranes, triggering NLRP3 inflammasome activation, release of IL-1 beta and TNF-alpha, fibroblast proliferation, and formation of concentric whorled hyalinized fibrotic 'silicotic nodules'. (PMID 41862874)
- Chest radiography classically demonstrates multiple small, rounded opacities (1–10 mm) predominantly distributed in the upper lung zones; peripheral 'eggshell' calcification of hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes is a characteristic radiographic sign highly suggestive of silicosis. (PMID 41526184)
- Clinical variants include: Chronic simple silicosis (develops after >10-20 years of low-level exposure; often asymptomatic initially), Accelerated silicosis (develops within 5-10 years of heavy exposure, common in artificial stone workers), and Acute silicoproteinosis (develops within months of massive exposure, featuring alveolar filling with lipoproteinaceous material mimicking pulmonary alveolar proteinosis). (PMID 37349198)
- Silicosis confers an enormous (up to 30-fold) increased lifetime risk of developing pulmonary tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis) due to silica-induced impairment of alveolar macrophage antimicrobial defenses; all patients with silicosis must undergo screening for latent tuberculosis with annual testing. (PMID 39578762)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy of whole lung lavage in clearing alveolar particulate burden in rapidly progressive acute and accelerated artificial stone silicosis.
- Role of antifibrotic medications (nintedanib or pirfenidone) in slowing lung functional decline in progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Infectious vulnerability in silicosis: silica disrupts alveolar macrophage function, conferring a dramatically elevated risk of active Tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis).
- Pathognomonic imaging sign: 'eggshell' calcification of hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes combined with upper-lobe predominant small rounded nodules.
- Modern occupational surge: artificial engineered stone countertop cutters and polishers develop rapidly progressive accelerated silicosis within years of exposure.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 34-year-old kitchen countertop fabricator working with engineered quartz stone presenting with 6 months of rapidly progressive exertional dyspnea and bilateral upper-lobe coalescent masses.
- A 62-year-old retired hard-rock miner with chronic silicosis presenting with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and a new cavitary lesion inside an upper-lobe conglomerate mass.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1620] Silo Filler's Disease

**Cluster**: silo filler's disease | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Silo filler's disease is an inhalational injury from nitrogen dioxide released by fermenting silage. It causes acute pneumonitis and, in some patients, delayed bronchiolitis obliterans.

### Core Teaching Points
- Fermenting silage releases nitrogen oxides; nitrogen dioxide reacts with water in the airway to form nitric and nitrous acids, damaging epithelium and the alveolar-capillary barrier. (PMID 42001620)
- Exposure can cause immediate cough and bronchospasm, pulmonary oedema or ARDS within hours, and a delayed bronchiolitis obliterans 2 to 6 weeks later. (PMID 42001620)
- Management is removal from exposure, oxygen, supportive care and ventilation if needed; systemic corticosteroids are used on expert opinion, particularly for the delayed phase, since controlled evidence is lacking. (PMID 32870425)
- Prevention relies on ventilating silos, entry precautions for the first weeks after filling and respiratory protection. (PMID 32870425)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with silo filler's disease.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles

- Triphasic course including delayed bronchiolitis.
- Prevention measures.

## [1621] Sinusoidal Obstruction Syndrome

**Cluster**: sinusoidal obstruction syndrome | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), formerly known as hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD), is a life-threatening endothelial complication predominantly occurring following myeloablative hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Toxic injury to sinusoidal endothelial cells produces post-sinusoidal portal hypertension and rapid multi-organ failure.

### Core Teaching Points
- Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS/VOD) is initiated by toxic conditioning chemotherapy (high-dose cyclophosphamide, busulfan, or total body irradiation) damaging hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells and hepatocytes in zone 3 of the liver acinus, leading to sinusoidal microthrombosis, subendothelial edema, and post-sinusoidal portal hypertension. (PMID 41530538)
- The classic clinical triad—typically developing within 21 to 30 days post-HSCT—features painful tender hepatomegaly, rapid unexplained weight gain secondary to fluid retention/ascites, and hyperbilirubinemia (jaundice). (PMID 40880758)
- Diagnostic criteria (European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation [EBMT] or modified Seattle criteria) establish clinical diagnosis without requiring invasive liver biopsy; Doppler ultrasound assists diagnosis by revealing portal venous flow reversal (hepatofugal flow), elevated hepatic arterial resistive index (>0.75), and gallbladder wall edema. (PMID 40914395)
- Defibrotide—a polydisperse oligonucleotide with protective endothelial, antithrombotic, and profibrinolytic properties without systemic anticoagulant bleeding risks—is the only approved, life-saving therapy for severe SOS/VOD, significantly improving survival and complete response rates when initiated early. (PMID 39258505)
- Risk factors include myeloablative conditioning regimens, preexisting liver disease or cirrhosis, prior gemtuzumab ozogamicin or inotuzumab ozogamicin exposure, HLA-mismatched or unrelated allogeneic donors, and active viral hepatitis. (PMID 41703584)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal threshold for defibrotide prophylaxis in pediatric and adult patients receiving high-risk conditioning regimens.
- Transjugular hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG >=10 mmHg) utility versus clinical diagnostic scoring in equivocal early presentation.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Clinical triad of hepatic SOS/VOD: painful hepatomegaly, fluid retention/rapid weight gain with ascites, and hyperbilirubinemia occurring post-HSCT.
- Specific pharmacological treatment of choice: defibrotide possesses endothelial-protective and local profibrinolytic actions, reducing mortality in severe SOS.
- Doppler ultrasound hemodynamic feature: reversal of portal venous flow (hepatofugal flow) confirms severe post-sinusoidal portal hypertension.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 42-year-old woman on day 16 following allogeneic stem cell transplantation for AML who gains 4 kg in 48 hours, develops right upper quadrant pain, ascites, and total bilirubin 5.4 mg/dL.
- A 28-year-old male with severe acute hepatic SOS post-busulfan conditioning initiated on intravenous defibrotide 6.25 mg/kg every 6 hours.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1622] Six-Minute Walk Test

**Cluster**: six minute walk test | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
The Six-Minute Walk Test (6MWT) is a standardized, self-paced, submaximal exercise test evaluating integrated functional exercise capacity in cardiopulmonary diseases. Widely utilized in pulmonary arterial hypertension, COPD, and heart failure, the 6MWT serves as a key clinical trial endpoint and prognostic biomarker.

### Core Teaching Points
- The 6MWT measures the total distance (in meters) that a patient can walk quickly on a flat, hard, straight, enclosed corridor (ideally 30 meters in length) over a period of 6 minutes, reflecting global integrated cardiopulmonary, neuromuscular, and metabolic functional capacity. (PMID 41027267)
- Standardized testing methodology (American Thoracic Society / European Respiratory Society technical guidelines) requires uniform pre-test rest (10 minutes), standardized neutral encouragement phrases spoken at exact 1-minute intervals, continuous pulse oximetry monitoring, and pre- and post-test Borg Dyspnea and Fatigue Scale ratings. (PMID 33064231)
- The Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) in 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) is approximately 30 to 33 meters across chronic respiratory and pulmonary vascular conditions (COPD, interstitial lung disease, and pulmonary arterial hypertension). (PMID 38869839)
- In pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), 6MWD is a core variable in comprehensive multi-parametric risk stratification tools (REVEAL 2.0 and ESC/ERS risk scores): a walk distance >440 meters signifies low 1-year mortality (<5%), whereas <165 to 320 meters signifies high risk (>20% mortality). (PMID 35062542)
- Exertional oxygen desaturation during the 6MWT—defined as an SpO2 drop >=4% or nadir SpO2 <88%—is an independent predictor of mortality and acute exacerbation in COPD and fibrotic interstitial lung disease, and guides prescription of ambulatory supplemental oxygen. (PMID 40769593)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Equivalence and reproducibility of automated wearable smartwatch/accelerometer step counts compared to clinic-based 30-meter hallway 6MWT.
- Prognostic significance of the desaturation distance ratio (DDR) versus absolute walking distance in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID): an improvement or decline of ~30–33 meters reflects a clinically meaningful change in functional exercise capacity.
- Prognostic cutoff in pulmonary arterial hypertension: 6MWD >440 meters is classified as a low-risk green-zone target predicting low 1-year mortality.
- Standardized test protocol adherence: standardized neutral phrases (e.g., 'You are doing well, you have 4 minutes left') must be used to avoid bias from uneven encouragement.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 52-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis whose 6MWD drops from 420 meters to 360 meters over 6 months with an exertional desaturation nadir of 84%.
- A 40-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis-associated PAH whose 6MWD improves by 55 meters following 12 weeks of dual oral endothelin receptor antagonist and PDE-5 inhibitor therapy.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1623] Sjogren syndrome: sicca symptoms, anti-Ro, anti-La, MALT lymphoma risk, systemic features

**Cluster**: sjogren syndrome sicca symptoms anti ro anti la malt lymphoma risk systemic features | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Primary Sjogren syndrome causes sicca symptoms and systemic features. The 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria use a weighted score; the main risk is B-cell lymphoma, usually MALT type.

### Core Teaching Points
- The 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria need ocular or oral dryness symptoms and a score of 4 or more from: anti-SSA/Ro positivity (3), focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with focus score of 1 or more (3), ocular staining score of 5 or more (1), Schirmer 5 mm/5 min or less (1), unstimulated salivary flow 0.1 mL/min or less (1). (PMID 42001623)
- Sjogren syndrome carries roughly a 10- to 20-fold higher risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, mainly marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma of the parotid; predictors include persistent salivary gland swelling, palpable purpura, cryoglobulinaemia and low C4. (PMID 31562236)
- Extraglandular disease (interstitial lung disease, renal tubular acidosis, vasculitis, neuropathy) is treated with corticosteroids and immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, mycophenolate or rituximab. (PMID 31562236)
- Dryness is managed symptomatically with artificial tears, saliva stimulation and pilocarpine or cevimeline. (PMID 31562236)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with sjogren syndrome: sicca symptoms, anti-ro, anti-la, malt lymphoma risk, systemic features.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles

- Lymphoma predictors.
- Treatment of glandular versus systemic disease.

## [1624] Sjogren syndrome systemic and topical therapy

**Cluster**: sjogren syndrome systemic and topical therapy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Primary Sjogren syndrome is a systemic autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands producing sicca manifestations (xerophthalmia and xerostomia), alongside extraglandular systemic involvement. Therapy combines topical tear/saliva substitutes and secretagogues with targeted systemic immunosuppression for extraglandular disease.

### Core Teaching Points
- Diagnosis of primary Sjogren syndrome requires objective demonstration of ocular or oral dryness (Schirmer test <=5 mm/5 min, ocular surface lissamine green staining) combined with positive anti-SSA/Ro autoantibodies (present in 70–80%) or focal lymphocytic sialadenitis on minor labial salivary gland biopsy (focus score >=1 per 4 mm2). (PMID 42719096)
- Topical symptomatic management of sicca symptoms includes preservative-free artificial tears, topical ophthalmic cyclosporine 0.05% drops (suppresses conjunctival lymphocyte activation and improves tear production), and artificial saliva sprays/gels. (PMID 40056051)
- Muscarinic receptor agonists—oral pilocarpine (5 mg three to four times daily) or cevimeline (30 mg three times daily)—stimulate residual functional salivary and lacrimal tissue via M3 receptors, significantly improving oral and ocular dryness; side effects include diaphoresis, flushing, nausea, and urinary frequency. (PMID 31672775)
- Systemic extraglandular manifestations (affecting 30–50% of patients) involve systemic vasculitis, interstitial lung disease, tubulointerstitial nephritis, peripheral neuropathy, and autoimmune cytopenias, requiring systemic immunosuppression with corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine (for arthralgias/fatigue), mycophenolate mofetil, or B-cell depletion with rituximab. (PMID 42067941)
- Patients with Sjogren syndrome carry a 15- to 20-fold increased lifetime risk of developing B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (predominantly marginal zone MALT lymphoma of the parotid gland or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma); clinical warning signs include persistent salivary gland enlargement, palpable purpura, cryoglobulinemia, and low serum complement C4. (PMID 40105662)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy of novel targeted B-cell therapies (anti-CD40, BAFF/APRIL inhibitors like ianalumab) in halting progressive exocrine gland destruction in early disease.
- Prognostic biomarkers predicting transition from benign lymphoepithelial sialadenitis to malignant marginal zone B-cell lymphoma.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Malignancy complication risk: Sjogren syndrome has the highest relative risk of lymphoma (~15-20 fold) among all autoimmune diseases, primarily MALT and DLBCL.
- Oral secretagogue mechanism: pilocarpine and cevimeline are M3 muscarinic receptor agonists that enhance salivation and lacrimation.
- Ophthalmic topical therapy: topical cyclosporine 0.05% eye drops reduce local ocular surface inflammation and increase tear volume.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 48-year-old woman with dry gritty eyes, severe dry mouth requiring water to swallow dry crackers, and positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, started on oral pilocarpine 5 mg TID.
- A 56-year-old woman with longstanding Sjogren syndrome who develops firm, painless, persistent unilateral swelling of the left parotid gland and palpable lower-extremity purpura.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1625] Skin and soft tissue infection antibiotic strategy

**Cluster**: skin and soft tissue infection antibiotic strategy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) range from superficial non-purulent cellulitis to life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis. Antimicrobial strategy is guided by distinguishing purulent from non-purulent infections, identifying systemic signs of toxicity, and recognizing necrotizing emergency features.

### Core Teaching Points
- Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines classify SSTIs fundamentally into non-purulent infections (cellulitis, erysipelas) and purulent infections (furuncles, carbuncles, abscesses), subdivided into mild, moderate, and severe based on systemic inflammatory signs. (PMID 24973422)
- Non-purulent cellulitis and erysipelas are overwhelmingly caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci (predominantly Streptococcus pyogenes [Group A Strep]); empirical therapy targets Streptococcus with beta-lactams (oral flucloxacillin, cefalexin, or IV cefazolin); coverage for MRSA is NOT routinely required in typical non-purulent cellulitis unless systemic toxicity, penetrating trauma, or prior MRSA carriage is present. (PMID 40343914)
- Purulent SSTIs (subcutaneous abscesses) are primarily caused by Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA); primary treatment for mild simple abscesses is incision and drainage alone without routine antibiotics; adjunctive oral antibiotics (TMP-SMX or doxycycline for CA-MRSA) are added for systemic symptoms, multiple abscesses, severe surrounding cellulitis, or immunocompromised hosts. (PMID 38626068)
- Severe SSTI with systemic toxicity (fever, hypotension, leukocytosis) or rapid spread mandates hospitalization and broad-spectrum intravenous coverage: vancomycin or daptomycin (for MRSA) plus piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime (for gram-negative bacilli). (PMID 36669559)
- Necrotizing soft tissue infections (necrotizing fasciitis) are surgical emergencies requiring immediate emergent operative debridement; clinical red flags include pain out of proportion to physical findings, rapid progression across demarcated borders, skin bullae/necrosis, palpable subcutaneous gas (crepitus), and sensory anesthesia. (PMID 28073795)
- In suspected necrotizing fasciitis, empiric antimicrobial therapy must include clindamycin (600–900 mg IV q8h) combined with broad-spectrum agents (vancomycin plus meropenem/piperacillin-tazobactam); clindamycin functions as a protein synthesis inhibitor that suppresses the production of Staphylococcal and Streptococcal superantigen toxins (Eagle effect). (PMID 24973422)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Safety and efficacy of single-dose long-acting lipoglycopeptides (dalbavancin, oritavancin) in outpatient management of moderate-to-severe SSTIs.
- Optimal duration of antimicrobial therapy (5 days vs 10 days) for uncomplicated cellulitis achieving early clinical stability.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Empirical therapy for typical non-purulent cellulitis: beta-lactams targeting Group A Streptococcus (flucloxacillin, cefalexin, or cefazolin); routine MRSA coverage is NOT necessary.
- Management of simple cutaneous abscess: incision and drainage alone is curative; antibiotics provide no benefit in uncomplicated single abscesses without systemic signs.
- Toxin suppression in necrotizing fasciitis: clindamycin is added to shut down bacterial ribosome translation and halt Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome exotoxin production.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 54-year-old woman presenting with a rapidly spreading, warm, tender, well-demarcated erythematous plaque over the right lower leg with tinea pedis, without purulence or systemic signs.
- A 42-year-old diabetic man presenting with severe agonizing right thigh pain out of proportion to a patch of erythema, with tachycardia, fever, and skin crepitus on palpation.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 40343914**: *Correction: Antimicrobial resistance in bacterial wound, skin, soft tissue and surgical site infections in Central, Eastern, Southern and Western Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis.* (2025) [meta-analysis] - PLOS global public health

## [1626] Sleep apnoea and cardiovascular disease: CPAP, AF risk, hypertension, arrhythmia

**Cluster**: sleep apnoea and cardiovascular disease cpap af risk hypertension arrhythmia | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Obstructive sleep apnoea is a recognised cause of resistant hypertension and is associated with atrial fibrillation. CPAP lowers blood pressure modestly; evidence that it prevents cardiovascular events is not established.

### Core Teaching Points
- Obstructive sleep apnoea raises sympathetic activity and is a common secondary cause of resistant hypertension. (PMID 42001626)
- CPAP lowers blood pressure by a few mmHg, with larger effects in resistant hypertension and with good adherence. (PMID 28115644)
- Treating sleep apnoea may reduce atrial fibrillation recurrence after cardioversion or ablation, though randomised data are mixed. (PMID 28115644)
- Large randomised trials (for example SAVE) did not show that CPAP reduces major cardiovascular events overall. (PMID 28115644)
- Nocturnal bradyarrhythmias related to apnoea often improve with CPAP, so permanent pacing is deferred if they occur only during sleep-disordered breathing. (PMID 42001626)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with sleep apnoea and cardiovascular disease: cpap, af risk, hypertension, arrhythmia.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles

## [1627] SLE: SLICC 2012 and ACR/EULAR 2019 classification criteria compared

**Cluster**: sle slicc 2012 and acr eular 2019 classification criteria compared | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
The 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria require ANA positivity at 1:80 or above and a weighted score of 10 points or more with at least one clinical criterion. The 2012 SLICC criteria need four criteria including one clinical and one immunological, or biopsy-proven lupus nephritis with ANA or anti-dsDNA.

### Core Teaching Points
- The 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria require ANA of 1:80 or higher as entry, then weighted points across 7 clinical and 3 immunological domains; 10 points or more classifies SLE, with sensitivity about 96% and specificity about 93%. (PMID 42001627)
- The 2012 SLICC criteria classify SLE when at least four criteria (one clinical, one immunological) are met, or biopsy-proven lupus nephritis is present with ANA or anti-dsDNA antibodies. (PMID 42001627)
- In the 2019 criteria, class III or IV lupus nephritis carries the highest weight (10 points), so ANA positivity plus such a biopsy is enough for classification. (PMID 31562236)
- Classification criteria are for research cohorts, not substitutes for clinical diagnosis. (PMID 31562236)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with sle: slicc 2012 and acr/eular 2019 classification criteria compared.
